articles.title: Canada's top court largely upholds Quebec ban on religious symbols for public servants
articles.summary: The law faced legal challenges from a range of groups, including female Muslim, Sikh and Catholic teachers, who argued it violated their fundamental rights.
body: Canada's top court has largely upheld a Quebec law banning public sector workers from wearing religious symbols, including the hijab and the cross.
The law, known as Bill 21, faced legal challenges from a range of groups, including female Muslim, Sikh and Catholic teachers, who argued it violated their fundamental rights.

Quebec passed the law in 2019 under a unique fixture of Canada's constitution called the "notwithstanding clause" - a legal loophole that allows governments to override certain rights, like freedom of religion.
The Supreme Court's decision is one of the most closely watched in Canadian history, with an impact that will be felt both in Quebec and across the country.

Reacting to the ruling on CBC, Prime Minister Mark Carney said his government would study its implications, adding it was important for all legislatures "to respect the rights and liberties of all Canadians, including those in the minority."

The Supreme Court was asked to weigh in on a number of questions, including on the constitutionality of Bill 21, whether Quebec's use of the notwithstanding clause was appropriate, and whether there are limits to its use.

On Friday, the top court confirmed the validity of Bill 21, but ruled that the law infringes on democratic rights by banning Quebec's elected officials from wearing a face covering for religious reasons.

The court also ruled that a Canadian court has the power to declare whether a law is consistent with the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms even if the notwithstanding clause is invoked, but that they would not do so in this case.
While the majority of the seven justices found that Quebec's law is largely valid, some dissented to parts of the decision.

Justices Andromache Karakatsanis, Michelle O'Bonsawin and Nicholas Kasirer wrote that the notwithstanding clause "cannot be used to authorize laws that are incompatible with the fundamental character of Canada as a free and democratic country".
Specifically, they said they believe the law infringes on the charter's guarantee to freedom of religion, freedom of expression and the right to equality.
What to know about the Supreme Court decision on Quebec's secularism bill

Civil liberty groups in Quebec have criticised Bill 21, saying it disproportionately affects Muslim women who wear the hijab, arguing that it has excluded them from key areas of public life in the province.
Stephen Brown, CEO of the National Council of Canadian Muslims, called the law "discriminatory" and criticised the court's decision.
"Entire categories of people are now barred from entire sectors of employment, not because of what they have done, but because of who they are," he said.
The chair of the English Montreal School Board, one of the main groups challenging the law, said the board was "obviously very disappointed" with the ruling.
"It wasn't the result we were looking for," Ortona told reporters. "But we do take solace from a lot of the declarations that were made by the court."
Quebec has argued that the law is necessary to uphold the province's state secularism - or laïcité - as a core component of its identity.

Earlier this year, the province passed another bill expanding its secularism rules to subsidised daycares and post-secondary institutions. It also restricted public prayer with fines for non-compliance.
The leader of the Bloc Québécois, a federal party that advocates for Quebec sovereignty, said Friday's ruling upheld the province's right to protect its values.

"We are now more than ever in a position to move forward with the preservation of the very elements that profoundly define the distinct nature of Quebec society," Yves-François Blanchet told reporters in French.
Watch: Isolation or neutrality: The cost of Quebec's secular law

articles.title: Kenyan doomsday cult leader convicted over further 123 deaths
articles.summary: Paul Mackenzie is found guilty of killing his followers, weeks after being jailed for the mass murder of children.
body: The self-styled pastor was arrested in 2023 after the discovery of more than 400 bodies in shallow graves
A court in Kenya has convicted the leader of a doomsday Christian cult of the manslaughter of 123 of his followers.
Paul Mackenzie was found guilty in Mombasa of ordering his followers, all adults, to fast to death in Shakahola forest near the coast between January 2021 and September 2023.
Earlier this month Mackenzie was jailed for 200 years for murdering 191 people, all but one of them children, in the same mass killing.
Mackenzie had pleaded not guilty to manslaughter and one of his lawyers said he would appeal against the conviction after sentencing, Reuters news agency reports.
Warning: This article contains details which some people might find distressing.
The court also convicted 29 others including Mackenzie's wife, Rhoda Mumbua Maweu, of their part in the manslaughter.
Sixty defendants were acquitted. The Director of Public Prosecutions indicated that an appeal would be launched against their acquittal.
The self-styled pastor was arrested in 2023 after the discovery of more than 400 bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola forest, near the Indian Ocean coast.

The court found Mackenzie had "systematically persuaded his followers to fast until they died", Kenya's Office of The Director of Public Prosecutions said in a statement on Friday's verdict, which it described as "the final conviction" in the cases against him.
"Children were to go first, then women and then men, with Mackenzie himself meant to die last," the office said.
The prosecution argued that Mackenzie and his accomplices had acted together as part of a suicide pact to fast to death in order to "meet Jesus".
Witnesses testified that he had preached that education, medicine and ornaments were sinful.
Those who opposed his teachings were beaten to death, according to the verdict in his trial for the murder of 191 people.
The defendants had claimed that the victims had fasted out of their own free will.
Earlier this week, Mackenzie was also convicted of:
assault causing actual bodily harm and five counts of cruelty to a child
engaging in organised criminal activity
facilitating the commission of a terrorist act
being in possession of an article connected with an offence under Kenya's Prevention of Terrorism Act, 2012.
Kenya cult leader who told parents to starve children guilty of 191 murders
Mackenzie established Good News International Ministries in 2003. Over the next 16 years, the church grew in popularity to draw thousands of followers in branches across Kenya.
A television station called Times TV would broadcast his sermons from his church in the resort town of Malindi.
His End Days sermons included conspiracy theories that described education as "evil", healthcare as "against the doctrine" and digital identity cards as "the mark of the devil".
After the main church shut down in 2019, Mackenzie moved to Shakahola forest, encouraging his devotees to follow him.
The community was described as mud houses scattered across the vast forest.
"We lived a quiet normal life, fasting for a few days then having a small meal," said survivor Peter Shukrani, who was rescued after falling ill.
Stephen Mwiti, who lost six children to the cult, welcomed the conviction of Mackenzie for murder last month
When the shallow graves were discovered, local men were hired for the horrifying task of exhuming the remains.
"Every grave we found had at least three bodies," James, one of the gravediggers, told the BBC. "Some of the remains were of children as young as a few weeks old."
"We once found 12 bodies of children in a line inside a grave. It was massive, the bodies were arranged like clothes. One on top of another."
Gravediggers described some of the bodies of children as having had their "hands and legs tied and bodies wrapped in bedsheets".
Post-mortem records showed many of the victims had died of starvation while the remains of others were mostly skeletal, making the establishment of their cause of death impossible.
Stephen Mwiti, 48, said he had lost all six of his children to the cult. His former wife was one of those convicted of murder alongside Mackenzie.
"I'm a happy man, that all persons have been convicted," he told the BBC outside court last month.
"All six of my children died in Shakahola forest. I only found and buried the remains of my son Samuel."
The deaths have shone a spotlight on the lack of oversight of rogue religious activities and how they could have carried on for so long.
The gravity of the case prompted President William Ruto to set up a commission of inquiry, although this was later declared unconstitutional.

articles.title: Millions of wives in South Asia unprotected from marital rape - study
articles.summary: More than 100 countries have outlawed marital rape, but a large part of South Asia has not.
body: Millions of women and girls remain unprotected in South Asia because of inadequate laws to deal with marital rape

Failure to fully criminalise marital rape leaves millions of women and girls unprotected in eight South Asian countries, where intimate partner violence is 35% higher than the global average, says a new study.
More than 100 countries have outlawed marital rape, but a large part of South Asia - India, Afghanistan, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh - remain among the three dozen countries which haven't.
The only South Asian country where rape within marriage attracts the same penalty as any other rape is The Maldives.
Nepal and Bhutan have criminalised marital rape, but apply lesser penalties, says the study by Samaj, a coalition of women's rights groups in the region.
India is among the three dozen countries where marital rape is still not outlawed
South Asia's marital rape laws largely stem from British colonial rule, says Ranjeeta Silwal of Equality Now, a global women's rights group part of Samaj.
The law, dating to 1860 in India and Bangladesh and 1885 in Sri Lanka, lists exceptions to rape - including sex by a man with his adult wife.
Campaigners say the law is outdated and forced sex is rape, regardless of the perpetrator. Experts warn marital sexual violence harms women's physical, psychological, emotional and sexual well-being.
More than 100 countries have criminalised marital rape, including the UK, which changed its law in 1991. But the exemption remains in India, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh.
In India, growing clamour to criminalise rape within marriage
Marital rape: Delhi high court gives split verdict
India government says criminalising marital rape 'excessively harsh'

Pakistan removed the marital rape exception in 2006, but no higher court has confirmed that rape laws apply within marriage. A recent high court ruling, meanwhile, granted husbands broad immunity for non-consensual sex.
Since returning to power in 2021, the Taliban have steadily dismantled women's protections in Afghanistan.

A new penal code introduced in January made matters worse, Silwal says. Under it, a husband can be prosecuted for violence against his wife only if he causes a broken bone, open wound or severe bruising. Even then, he faces just 15 days in prison if convicted.
Unsurprisingly, the code makes no mention of marital rape. But its narrow definition of punishable violence effectively denies women protection against it.
Intimate partner violence is much higher than the global average in South Asian countries
"The idea comes from the belief that consent for sex is implied in marriage, that marriage is a threshold where consent ends," Silwal told the BBC.
"But it shows a lack of awareness, it shows we are still treating women as property, that we are still very patriarchal."
The report comes amid renewed debate over marital rape across the region.
In India, 10 petitions challenging the law are pending before the Supreme Court, which is due to begin final hearings on 9 December.
Courts have delivered contradictory rulings over the years, with some judges acknowledging the law's archaic nature and urging parliament to criminalise marital rape.
There was outrage last year when a court let go a man whose wife had died after he brutally raped her.
But the Indian government, religious organisations and men's rights activists have opposed petitions in the top court, saying criminalisation of marital rape would be "excessively harsh".
India refuses to criminalise marital rape. This new series shines a light on it
India anger as judge frees man accused of raping wife who then died

Rights groups in Bangladesh have also challenged the marital rape exception, arguing it violates constitutional rights to life, liberty and protection from torture and cruel treatment, the report says.
"Those who oppose criminalising marital rape say it would undermine the family unit and break them apart. And family is very important in our countries," Silwal says.
"They say it will affect our religious and cultural values and worry that there would be false accusations against men."
Also a change in law, she says, may not necessarily mean justice for survivors.
Silwal points to Bhutan where marital rape is a criminal offence but it's treated as a petty misdemeanour and is punishable by one month to one year.
In Nepal, the punishment for rape is between six and 20 years, but it's only up to five years for a husband who rapes his wife.

articles.title: Weary of war but with no sign of backing down, Kyiv faces another punishing winter
articles.summary: Ukraine settles in for another devastating winter as the questions persists: how will it all end?
body: Weary of war but with no sign of backing down, Kyiv faces another punishing winter

Something weird happens when you reach Kyiv after the eight-hour drive from the Polish border: the clock on your mobile phone goes to midnight. It's not really for phones - it seems to be part of a wider strategy to disorient the missiles and drones the Russians are sending over.

Aside from little things like that, though, Kyiv seems fairly normal at first sight. You become well aware there's a war on when sirens begin to wail and people check their phones for the notifications which tell them there's a red alert and missiles are on their way. You can even buy gadgets that show you which direction the drones are coming from, and what type they are.

The drones and ballistic missiles have been hitting in sizeable numbers over the last couple of weeks. On the morning of Monday 16 November, the battle of the bridges began. Ukraine hit the Kerch bridge which links Russia to illegally occupied Crimea. Then it launched a bigger wave of missiles and drones, damaging the central road-bridge arch. A few hours later, presumably in revenge, Russia fired seven ballistic missiles at Kyiv, disabling two of the nine bridges that cross the River Dnipro.

The war has dragged on for more than four and a half years, killing what some estimate could be 100,000 Ukrainian troops and 18,000 Ukrainian civilians, according to the United Nations, and probably more. Its infrastructure, too, has been battered, as well as its morale. While temperatures drop to freezing at night, and with Ukrainians regularly suffering from no light, heat or water thanks to Russian strikes, can the country survive another difficult winter under bombardment? And what would a peace deal, if one could be struck, look like?

Kyiv is mostly dark at night, thanks to Russia's campaign of targeting Ukraine's electricity generating capability. In the blackness last week, the air raid sirens started wailing across the city, and our hotel's warning announcements came over the loudspeakers. Within a few minutes, we heard the first explosions. I jumped out of bed and stared out of the window into the darkness. After a few seconds two more missiles landed, lighting up the entire sky momentarily in a blaze of white and red. They were uncomfortably close.

Many people prefer to go to the shelters when there's a red alert. Others just stay in bed and hope the law of averages will protect them. It usually does. During one of the heaviest attacks last week, the number of fatalities was in single figures.

I went to the shelter in our hotel one night. The clearly audible thumps and crashes above ground, the permanent lighting, the snores and grunts of other people, and the attentions of the little biting flies that seem to thrive in the warm, crowded shelters made sleep hard.
Kyiv is entering its fourth winter following Russia's full-scale invasion

To the people who live here in Kyiv, it's frightening, certainly, if a drone or a missile hits close by, but enraging too. Over the years I've been in several cities that were being bombed by high-tech weaponry and the reaction always seems the same, whether it's Lebanon, Iraq, Serbia, or Ukraine: a combination of weariness and fury. In Kyiv the attacks come by night and day, making normal life almost impossible. An uninterrupted night's sleep is a rarity. The morning after the bridges were hit, people in the streets looked tired and worn.

Yet although they long for it to stop, there's no sign they want Ukraine to surrender. On the contrary, just about everyone I spoke to felt they had to keep fighting. That's borne out by an opinion poll last month by the KIIS organisation, a Ukrainian market research company, which found that 62% of people were prepared to put up with the war for as long as it took. Of those polled, 79% believed that Ukraine would win the war in the long run, and only 7% thought Russia would win. These aren't the reactions of a country which is being beaten to its knees.

I don't have any doubt that Ukraine can survive the winter. Food is plentiful, though prices are high. Water is a problem, because the regular attacks on the power grid mean that it can't be pumped with any regularity. Kyiv underwent a large transformation under the Soviets, so there are large numbers of high-rise blocks of flats everywhere. Labouring up and down the stairs when there's no power is daunting, especially when you've got to carry quantities of water home.

We came across a small crowd of people in their 20s who had gathered outside a nightclub for a rave at three in the afternoon, because of the 11pm curfew. "It's a way of getting a bit of respite from everything," said one young woman. "It makes me feel I can put up with everything," said a man.

Do people still support President Volodymyr Zelensky? My team and I met an elderly woman wandering around Independence Square in the centre of Kyiv holding a photo of her son, who was missing on the Eastern front. She blamed Zelensky; if he didn't insist on carrying on the war, she believed, her son would still be alive. It isn't a response most people seem to share. The same polling organisation, KIIS, found that Zelensky's trust ratings hover around 54% to 57% — way below the 90% he was registering in the early days of the war in 2022, but not too bad for a man who's been in power now for more than seven years.
Zelensky's ratings have dipped considerably

What comes across all the time in Kyiv is an absolute loathing of Russia. Putin reportedly launched his invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 because his intelligence chiefs assured him that Ukrainians longed to rejoin the Motherland.

Russian missiles have hit hospitals, clinics and schools. In many well-attested cases the Russians have used the "double-tap" method — sending in one missile, then waiting till the medics and rescuers gather before sending in another. At least 20,000 Ukrainian children have been abducted and taken to Russia, according to Ukraine's Ministry of Justice. In late March 2022, when the Ukrainians recaptured the satellite town of Bucha, on the outskirts of Kyiv, they found shocking evidence of torture and murder. Ukrainian soldiers call their Russian enemies Orcs, after the sub-human brutes in The Lord of the Rings. A country that has endured this kind of thing doesn't quickly forgive and forget. Russia denies that it targets civilians or civilian infrastructure.

Ukraine has never lost its own identity, even during the Soviet period. Some of Ukraine's culture was absorbed by Russia — "They call borsch [a famously delicious soup made of beetroot] theirs, but they got it from us," a waiter in a café here told me proudly. After the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, Ukraine overwhelmingly voted for independence. The war has brought a fierce renewal of this desire to be completely separated from Russia.

It's not my usual beat, but my team and I went to film on the set of MasterChef Ukraine, currently one of the country's favourite television programmes. The studio was borrowed; the original one had been bombed. The executive producer had his phone in his hand the whole time, and was constantly glancing at it. The moment a red alert showed, it was his duty to shepherd everyone off the set to a nearby shelter. "People see our cuisine as a way of expressing their national identity," he said. It's one of the reasons the programme is so popular.

There are other ways in which people express their Ukrainian national identity under the bombs. There has been a boom for books being written and published about Ukraine and Ukrainian identity. Ukrainian and Russian are close as languages, though vocabulary and pronunciation differ. Nowadays the differences are emphasised. "Woe betide a writer who uses Russian spellings," a Ukrainian novelist told me.

The war will end at some point; wars always do. But there has to be a clear winner before anyone backs down, and a lasting peace can be negotiated. US President Donald Trump and his advisers, people like Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, with their business backgrounds, have approached the situation as though it's a form of mergers and acquisitions: make a deal attractive enough, and the other side will accept it.

So, last week, Washington was rumoured to be offering a very Trumpian deal, that Ukraine should accept the loss of the land in the east which the Russians now control, and in return it was rumoured it could join Nato. It was a non-starter, because Russia would never accept it. The sweetener, in this US plan, was that the West's sanctions against Russia would be lifted, and both sides would benefit from unrestricted trading once again.

But neither side sees this as being about trade and profit. For Russia, it's about the dangers of being humiliated if it doesn't win. President Vladimir Putin has made it his personal war. By illegally taking Crimea from Ukraine in 2014, he made himself very popular in Russia. If he doesn't win this second stage of a 12-year campaign against Ukraine, the consequences for him personally could be disastrous. He's already had to face down one attempt against his rule: his former associate Yevgeny Prigozhin's march on Moscow in June 2023. In a much-quoted remark, reported last August, Putin is said to have confided to his associates that if he didn't win the war "they'll hang me". My sense is he's not concerned about trade with the West and the profit that will bring, so much as about his personal survival.

Similarly, Ukrainians aren't interested in the precise details that have leaked out of the various negotiations between the Americans and Russians. Their contempt for the US is immense; "they just failed us," said one Ukrainian I spoke to.

And they don't believe Russia will stick to any future peace agreement anyway. "They signed a treaty to accept our borders, and Putin broke it," a young man told me as he sat hunched over his laptop in a bookshop. "The only solution is to defeat them."
Tens of thousands of soldiers have died since the outbreak of war

Other people talked about the need to get huge reparations from Russia for the terrible destruction it has visited on their country. According to one estimate, reconstruction and recovery will cost more than $500bn (£383bn), an unthinkably huge amount for a country whose GDP was $200bn before the war. President Trump and his advisers don't seem to have addressed any of these issues in their negotiations.

Here in Kyiv, peace doesn't seem at all close. Russia's efforts to make life intolerable for Ukraine's citizens are certainly having a major effect. The war is often frightening for ordinary people, and it can be appallingly destructive of property and lives. But short of hugely escalating by attacking Ukraine with nuclear weapons, which is something China and the US are both thought to have warned him not to do, Putin can't seem to strike the knock-out blow against Ukraine that he needs.

At present it seems to people in Ukraine that the war will never come to an end. Yet it will, at some point: and then the crucial requirement will be to work out ways to stop Russia coming back for another round. One way would be if Ukraine joins Nato, but that's something Russia would only accept if it had been comprehensively defeated. Ukrainians might think that can happen, but most Western onlookers are more sceptical.

The daily and nightly sirens, the explosions of missiles and drones, the shortages and the fear and the darkness are all terrible. But they aren't enough to destroy Ukraine's will to continue fighting.

articles.title: Behind China's spectacular rise, voices who defied it say they are being drowned out
articles.summary: China's immense clout now also has the flex of soft power. Critics and dissidents say their voices are being drowned out.
body: China's economic might is drowning out our voices, say activists and dissidents
For Uyghur activist Dolkun Isa, who has lived in exile in Germany for nearly three decades, the thinning of the crowds is the clearest measure of how much his cause is slipping off the world's radar.
"Back in 2018, we could easily get thousands of people out in the streets to protest against China's human rights violations. Nowadays, we have trouble finding even 500."

It was in 2018 that reports emerged that China had detained up to a million Uyghurs and other Muslims in mass internment camps in its north-western province of Xinjiang. Beijing, which said the camps were for "re-education" to counter separatist violence, denied the allegations detailing alarming rights abuses.

But an international outcry, including protests, followed. Western governments rolled out trade bans and sanctions against senior Chinese officials, and froze their assets, and at least nine countries issued parliamentary resolutions condemning the detentions.
It was a time "when we felt the world was finally listening", says Dolkun, 59, who served as president of the Munich-based World Uyghur Congress from 2017-2024 .
But today, "we find ourselves competing against economic interests and geopolitical calculations to capture the world's attention. For me, this is one of the most painful aspects of our struggle".
Uyghur activist Dolkun Isa has lived in exile in Germany for nearly three decades

Few corners of the world remain untouched by China's rise. Its electric vehicles pack highways from Brazil to Belgium, made-in-China batteries, solar panels, AI models and microdramas fuel daily consumption in so many places, and Labubu dolls, Pop Mart's furry gap-toothed plush, dangle from backpacks almost everywhere.

China's immense economic clout now also has the flex of soft power, drowning out voices that say their fight against the Communist Party cannot compete with the country's gleaming skylines, advanced exports or futuristic ambitions.
Buoyed by its successes, Beijing is also swapping the "stick" for the "carrot", says Uyghur journalist Arslan Hidayat, who was born and raised in Australia, where he runs Kashgar Times.

Activists tell the BBC Beijing has been offering family reunions, money and the promise of safety - in return, they are asked for information about their networks and to promote pro-party narratives. The result, activists say, is a movement with fewer voices and less trust.
The Chinese embassy in the UK dismissed the activists' claims that they would be asked to spy on or disclose information about fellow exiles.
Sheznhen, a rich, buzzing city on the soth-eastern coast, has emerged as one of China's star attractions for tech and tourism
China's "economic muscle" has earned it respect abroad and reshaped foreign policy, says Ian Johnson, a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist who has long reported on Chinese civil society.
"At the same time, Western governments have become much more inwardly focused and populist, pushing human rights down their lists of priorities."

China's human rights record has not earned a mention in any of the three summits Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump held this year, including the one in Shenzhen last week. As Beijing's leverage on the global stage has grown, so has the cost of confrontation or condemnation.
This shift in Beijing's image and tactics is deeply worrying, dissidents say, because it is weakening both their networks and the international pressure they hope to build.

In July Tibetan activist Lobga Rangzen died after he set himself on fire outside the UN headquarters in New York. He was protesting against China's sweeping new "ethnic unity law" which, among other things, requires minorities, including Tibetans, to learn Mandarin. The UN called it an "absolutely tragic" incident, but attention quickly faded.

His death was "an appeal to the international community", says Tenzin Dorjee, a researcher at the Tibet Action Institute, but he thinks much of the world is reluctant to criticise China because of the power it wields.
That same month Dolkun tried to rally supporters against the same law but he met with a muted response.
"Many people have dialled down on their activism over the years because they are thinking about their loved ones back in China," Dolkun says.
Donald Trump and Xi Jinping have held three summits so far this year
Arslan says he has interviewed at least a dozen Uyghur exiles who were "invited to go back to China on the condition that they would provide information to Chinese agents from time to time".
The questions seem "fairly innocuous", he adds: "Who lives around you? Which Uyghur restaurants do you frequent? We believe these are used to build out the profiles of dissidents overseas."
Beijing's embassy in the UK said in its response to the BBC that "facilitating visits to China by overseas Chinese to reunite with their families" is a "normal part" of consular services.
"China respects and protects the lawful rights and interests of people of all ethnic groups, including the Uyghurs, and their freedom to maintain contact with family members overseas," it added.
These family visits often happen in large groups and are well documented on China's official platforms.
In Turkey, which hosts tens of thousands of Muslim minorities from Xinjiang, Chinese Consul-General Wei Xiaodong was photographed sending off some 30 participants from Istanbul in January.
Consul-General Wei Xiaodong (in the red scarf) pictured sending people off in January

"He expressed hope that the diaspora returning to Xinjiang would experience the region's development... and would actively promote these developments upon their return to Turkey," read a post on the consulate's WeChat page.

Beijing has repackaged Xinjiang into a traveller's haven. The region saw more than 300 million domestic and international tourist visits last year, more than double the number in 2018, Chinese authorities say.
The post from China's Turkish consulate concluded with a clip showing loved ones hugging and presenting bouquets as they reunite with family at the airport in Urumqi, the capital of Xinjiang.
"People are happy to stay quiet and lay low for the little communication they've been allowed to establish with their loved ones," Arslan says.
Though the trips are publicised, it is unclear what makes someone eligible to participate in them. Some suggest that even dating histories come under the microscope.

Alim*, a Uyghur exiled in Turkey, says a friend who made an appeal to the consulate to consider her for a trip was rejected, with staffers alluding to her past relationship with a Kazakh man who at one point was "quite active" in lobbying for his parents who were detained in China.
"She was very eager to go on one of these 'family visits' because she hasn't seen her loved ones back home in so many years... She was crushed that she was rejected," says Alim.
"The way I understand it, the 'ideal participant' is someone influential enough to amplify China's messages, yet not associated with anything or anyone too political."
Xinjiang has been sold as an exotic destination, bringing in huge numbers of tourists
When Mehmut* was invited on a family visit in October 2024, he jumped at the opportunity.

The Uyghur businessman hoped a trip back to China would help him re-establish the links needed to "keep our business afloat". Far from the warm reunions Mehmut had expected, he says his engagement with friends and family "felt superficial".
"It was not like officials were actively monitoring me or restricting my movements. But there was a great dose of fear and self-censorship in my conversations with people," he says.
"Some were caught off guard to see me return, others appeared very cautious with what they told me. The experience just made me feel very uncomfortable."
These visits do not just serve Beijing's narrative; they also drive a wedge within communities, activists say.
Abduweli Ayup, a prominent Uyghur linguist based in Norway, has observed former activists going off the grid after returning from these trips.

"Some have deleted their social media accounts and cut off contact with us," he says. "Others appear to be suspicious of us or concerned that what we were doing would compromise theirs or their families' safety."
The fact that only a few get selected to visit the homeland "creates confusion within the diaspora," says Tibetan activist Karma Rinchen.
"They get sidelined when they return... Very sadly, our suspicions that some of them are feeding information back to the Chinese authorities have turned out to be true."
Karma Rinchen's parents were among thousands who fled Tibet alongside the Dalai Lama in 1959

Rinchen serves as information secretary in the Tibetan government-in-exile in the northern Indian town of Dharamshala. His parents were among thousands who followed their spiritual leader Dalai Lama into exile after China annexed Tibet.

Over the decades, waves of others have fled Chinese rule seeking greater freedom or asylum from Beijing's crackdowns - dissidents and student activists in the wake of the Tiannanmen Square massacre; lawyers, journalists, purged officials and critics in the years after, and, more recently, Hong Kong saw a steady exodus build as the pro-democracy movement was crushed.
Many have kept on fighting. But now, they say, Beijing's might is chipping away at their struggle, making it ever harder to stand up to the Chinese Communist Party.

"Many among us have been separated from our families for generations and are eager to set foot on Tibet soil," Rinchen says. "This is exactly the kind of desperation the Communist Party seeks to target."
But he adds this only means communities have to "work harder to make sure their voices are heard".
A memorial for Tibetan activist Lobga Rangzen who set himself on fire outside the UN headquarters in New York

"For Tibetans, this is not something we can simply walk away from. Our struggle is about our identity, our culture, our religion and the basic rights of our people. We have been doing this work for many decades, and we have learned to remain patient and persistent," Rinchen adds.
For many, that persistence continues to be tested on a personal level.
Uyghur musician Mirkamel Tourghoun has lived as a refugee in Paris since 2008, spending most of his time writing music and making films about Uyghur culture.
The 42-year-old has chosen the painful path of cutting off contact with his family who remain in Urumqi.
In January, he received a call from someone claiming to be an official from the city.

articles.title: A clinic is reassessing people with ADHD and autism diagnoses - but critics fear it could deepen stigma
articles.summary: While many people find a diagnosis for ADHD or autism affirming, a government-funded clinic in Sweden is re-assessing people who feel it does not reflect them.
body: Johanna, 24, began questioning her ADHD diagnosis when she discovered it could act as a barrier to becoming a police officer
Freya looks nervous as she walks into a psychiatric clinic in Sweden for an ADHD assessment.
Countries around the world have seen a huge increase in ADHD diagnoses over recent decades. For many people this can be life changing, helping them understand themselves better and access support.
But Freya (not her real name) is not attending a long-awaited appointment to secure a diagnosis.
This government-funded clinic offers autism and ADHD diagnosis reassessments - its doctors believe it is the first in the world dedicated solely to this purpose.
At 12, Freya was struggling with anxiety at school and sought out professional help. "They thought I had ADHD," she says.
But as she grew up, she felt that she did not experience ADHD symptoms. "I don't think I had it in the first place," she now says.
Her doubts about the diagnosis became more pressing as a teenager, when she discovered that in Sweden, it could be a barrier to pursuing her dream career of joining the police.
"I want to have every option open," she tells BBC World Service.
If the doctors at the clinic decide Freya does not meet the ADHD criteria, her medical records will be updated, and it will be easier for her to apply for a job with the police.

The clinic, known as Mottagning Neuropsykiatri, has opened at a time when rates of ADHD and autism diagnoses are under the spotlight. Many say this is because of greater awareness of the symptoms, and that previously neglected groups - particularly women and girls - are finally getting the diagnoses they need, while others argue that the growing numbers stem from overdiagnosis.

The existence of the clinic is controversial. Clinical guidance from UK governing bodies and the World Health Organization describe autism as a lifelong condition and ADHD as a neurodevelopmental condition that can persist into adulthood. The medical consensus is that both diagnoses last a lifetime, even if symptoms fluctuate.

And some neurodiversity advocates warn that a dedicated reassessment service could reinforce the idea that being diagnosed with ADHD or autism is undesirable – and deepen the stigma surrounding both conditions.
Despite this, hundreds of people have approached the clinic about reassessment.
Psychologist Sebastian Lundström runs the clinic, which operates one day a month
Like Freya, other young adults have been prompted to reconsider their diagnosis after they felt it had become a barrier.

This is because historically, Swedes with ADHD or autism were barred from certain jobs, including joining the military, and becoming police officers, train drivers and pilots. This is despite research suggesting some neurodivergent traits can be strengths in certain roles. No such bans exist in the UK, although rules differ globally.

Since 2022, people with ADHD have been able to join the Swedish military if they are medication-free. And since 2021, people with ADHD or autism have been able to apply to join the police, but must submit a medical certificate, which can cost around 15,000 SEK (£1,100) privately.
When Freya was referred to the clinic, she says she was relieved to find out she could get her diagnosis reassessed there for free.
Johanna, 24, was diagnosed with ADHD at 14 after what she describes as a period of bad behaviour at school. She found the diagnosis helpful at first and received additional support from teachers.

But as she grew into adulthood, she says she stopped feeling that she needed extra support. And after discovering it was a barrier to becoming a police officer, she began questioning whether it was even accurate.
Johanna says she has some traits of ADHD, such as a short attention span, "but not enough to have an ADHD diagnosis," she believes.

Johanna was reassessed aged 21 during an early pilot of the reassessment clinic and was found not to meet its diagnostic criteria for ADHD. She now works for her father's company, and does not plan on becoming a police officer.

Both ADHD and autism are neurodevelopmental conditions that affect how people think and interact with the world. They are diagnosed through detailed assessments, which can include questionnaires and interviews, rather than one single clinical test.

The doctors at Mottagning Neuropsykiatri say their approach is different from traditional assessments, as it focuses less on someone's history, and more on the symptoms they are experiencing in the present.
"This is not de-diagnosing, this is a renewed assessment of your functioning today," says Sebastian Lundström, the clinic's lead psychologist.
The doctors say they do not judge whether the original assessment was correct, so rather than wiping the original diagnosis from patients' medical records, they add a note of the new assessment.

Lundström says that some people who once had a diagnosis but are found to not meet the criteria at the clinic may have been misdiagnosed. But he also believes that for a small minority, ADHD and autism are not lifelong conditions and individuals may stop experiencing symptoms as they grow older.
But updating a person's diagnosis because they are not currently showing symptoms is a contested approach.
"We have to remember that these are lifelong conditions," says Navid Ghannad, chair of Autism Skåne, a local Swedish non-profit for autistic people and their families.
"Because at a certain point in their adulthood during a clinical setting they have had their diagnosis removed, it doesn't necessarily mean that the ADHD or the autism has disappeared," he adds.

Symptoms could reappear later in life, he says. "The problem is once they resurface, that individual which doesn't have a diagnosis any longer, they will not be able to get the timely and correct support."
Lundström says he does not consider it a big risk that people could get reassessed and find themselves without necessary support.
During the pilot he encountered people who "really wanted" to get rid of their diagnoses but the psychologist said, "we still feel that you meet the criteria".
Vilda, 22, sought reassessment of her autism diagnosis as she feels she was misdiagnosed
Vilda, 22, sought reassessment of her autism diagnosis which was initially given after she experienced a trauma.
"I didn't recognise myself in the description of autism," she says. "I was stuck. I know that this is not me, but I can't do anything about it."
It was requests from people like Johanna and Vilda that led to the establishment of the clinic, Lundström explains.
"It gained momentum by itself and the word spread around. A lot of people contacted us and we felt that there was a justification for starting up," he says. It is only open one day a month.

Before opening the clinic, Lundström conducted a small peer-reviewed study - of the 72 individuals who took part, roughly 80% did not meet the criteria for ADHD or autism. All the participants already wanted to lose their diagnosis, rather than being a randomly selected group.
"It's important to stress that this patient population is not necessarily representative for all with autism and ADHD," he adds.

During the first year of the pilot some 400 to 500 people spoke to Lundström, who is also associate professor of child and adolescent psychiatric sciences at the University of Gothenburg, about getting a reassessment.
The project also has the backing of senior figures in Swedish psychiatry, including Sophia Eberhard, a senior consultant specialising in child and adolescent psychiatry.
"It's psychiatry who in the beginning made those diagnoses," she says. "I believe we have a responsibility to help these young adults on their way."
In September, the BBC was given permission to join Freya as she became the first patient to attend the newly opened clinic, which serves both men and women.

During her appointment, Freya takes part in questionnaires and verbal assessments to see if she meets the ADHD criteria. The process is the same for both ADHD and autism, although the questions differ.
Freya says she is hopeful that she will be able to "get rid" of her ADHD diagnosis after the appointment.

But the doctors are adamant that they do not just give attendees the outcome they want. They conduct other checks such as assessing body language and communication skills, speaking to younger patients' parents, and checking medical files for ongoing treatment.
Navid Ghannad, chair of Autism Skåne, a local Swedish non-profit for autistic people, says it is important to remember autism and ADHD are lifelong conditions
The opening of the clinic has drawn criticism from those who fear it sends the wrong message about autism and ADHD.

"The clinic presents neurodiversity and autistic people as a bad thing, like we are a problem that needs to be fixed - we are not," says Jenny Hedin, from charity Organiserade Autister Västernorrland, an advocacy organisation run by and for autistic adults.

Hedin, who is autistic and has ADHD, warns that people who can successfully "mask" or mimic neurotypical behaviour might feel under pressure to lose their diagnosis in order to be better accepted by society.
"That is especially a problem with women and girls, because girls are usually great at masking," she adds.
Others say the focus should be on changing the rules that make it difficult for people with ADHD or autism to pursue certain careers.
Eric Donell, the chairman of Riksförbundet Attention, a national Swedish charity, lobbies to remove employment restrictions affecting neurodivergent people, which he says are unfair.

He stresses that for many people, getting a diagnosis is extremely important. "Instead of asking people to get rid of their diagnosis, sometimes we should just ask whether the rules themselves are justified," he says.
Reassessments risk becoming "a way of adapting the individual to society instead of adapting society to human differences," he adds.
People from the UK, Denmark, Norway and Germany have also been in touch for reassessment, says Lundström, but they have been turned away, as the clinic only serves locals.
Georgina, 35, from the UK, contacted the clinic because she wants to have the autism diagnosis she received at 25 "removed".
"It felt like a magic spell, that I'd get this label and the world would be more understanding," she says.

articles.title: The Indian 'Tamasha queen' whose fans paid for a show that never happened
articles.summary: A new Bollywood flim spotlights the remarkable life of dancer and singer Vithabhai Narayangaonkar.
body: Vithabhai Narayangaonkar was a legend in Maharashtra's folk theatre
Few things could keep Vithabai Narayangaonkar, one of the greatest stars of Maharashtra's folk theatre, away from the stage.
Not even, it would seem, the birth of her child.
In the 1960s, the singer, dancer and troupe leader was performing in Shikhar Shingnapur, a village in the western Indian state, when she went into labour.
"She quietly stepped behind the stage into a makeshift tent while the rest of us continued performing," her daughter, veteran folk artist Mangala Bansode, told BBC Marathi.
Outside, the restless audience kept shouting: "Where is Vitha?"
When Vithabai returned to the stage, she was cradling her newborn son, the seventh of her eight children.
"The audience was stunned, but they quietly left, saying, 'We will watch your performance later'," Bansode recalled.

Outspoken and quick-witted, Vithabai held audiences across Maharashtra in thrall for decades, earning the title of Tamasha Samradnyi – the empress of Tamasha, the state's traditional travelling folk theatre.
Now, more than two decades after her death, her life has inspired a Bollywood musical, Eetha, starring Shraddha Kapoor, and due for release on 4 December.
Directed by Laxman Utekar, Eetha is based on Yogiraj Bagul's Marathi book chronicling Vithabai's life.

Rooted in devotional poetry, Tamasha evolved into a lively mix of music, dance, comedy and drama. At its heart is Lavani, a song and dance tradition in which verses ranging from the bawdy to the politically incisive are performed to the beat of the dholki, a percussion instrument.
Eetha evokes the world of Tamasha in its heyday. Kapoor, who had never performed Lavani before, learnt to dance while wearing musical anklets weighing 4kg each.
"The lives of Tamasha artists have been very tough, so in their dance you see pain as well as joy," Kapoor recalled at a promotional event.
Eetha hits the theatres on 5 December
Many Tamasha performers, including Vithabai, came from oppressed castes, facing discrimination even as their artistry drew large crowds.

How much of that history Eetha will capture remains debated. Utekar says it is not a biopic, but his decision to rename the protagonist Vithabai Bhau Gavkar instead of Vithabai Bhau Mang Narayangaonkar has drawn criticism.

For critics, much of Vithabai's history was contained in her name – Mang identified her with a historically oppressed Dalit community, while Narayangaonkar spoke of her family's roots in Narayangaon village. Both featured in the name of the troupe she inherited from her father – Bhau-Bapu Mang Narayangaonkar Tamasha Mandal.

Vithabai spoke openly about caste and the indignities Tamasha artists faced, themes that also surfaced in her songs. In a 1960s Lavani documented by historian Shailaja Paik, she rebuked men for lewd gestures, reminding them she danced to earn a living, not to please them.
It was a livelihood she had inherited from generations of performers in her family.
Like her son, Vithabai was born during a Tamasha performance, in 1935. Her mother, Shanta, had continued touring with her husband Bhau's troupe throughout her pregnancy.

Vithabai joined a theatre group at eight and her father's troupe at 13, soon becoming its star. After her father and co-leader Bapu died in quick succession, she took over the troupe with her husband and cousin.
Her career flourished during Tamasha's golden age, when productions grew more elaborate, drawing on mythology, history and contemporary life, says folk arts scholar Sukhada Khandge.
Khandge, who watched Vithabai perform as a child, recalls her sparkling eyes and commanding presence. She was as expressive with her face as she was with her feet.
Vithabai was known as the empress of Tamasha in Maharashtra
Her fame carried her beyond Maharashtra.

During India's war with China in 1962, Vithabai performed for soldiers in the North-East Frontier Agency, now largely Arunachal Pradesh, braving freezing conditions just three months after giving birth, Bansode says.
At a conference in 1996, she recalled meeting soldiers from the historically oppressed Mahar and Mang communities at the frontier.

"Our Mahar-Mang soldiers were expected to fight and lay down their lives defending the nation, but the very same people would not even allow our bridegroom to pass through the village entrance," she said.

Despite offers from leading filmmakers, including Raj Kapoor, and roles in Marathi cinema, Vithabai refused to leave theatre. Film fame, she felt, would benefit her alone, while her troupe supported some 50 families, Bansode says.
There was a tenderness, too, in her relationship with audiences.
In his book on Vithabai's life, which inspired Eetha, Yogiraj Bagul recounts a performance in Mumbai during Diwali in 1971.

Despite the threat of rain, spectators insisted on buying tickets, saying the money would be their Bhau Beej gift to Vithabai if the show was cancelled – a festival celebrating the bond between brothers and sisters.
When the rain came, people left chanting: "Bhau Beej, Bhau Beej."
No one asked for their money back.

But Vithabai's fortunes failed to match her fame. Her husband, Maruti Sawant, mismanaged the troupe's finances and took loans in her name, family members say. By the time she left him in 1982, she was heavily indebted.
Bagul also writes about a 1986 column in a Marathi daily that revealed how the empress of Tamasha was now travelling on public buses and staying in cheap accommodation.
Despite drawing huge crowds, Lavni dancers were often disdained
Despite public support, Vithabai was forced to disband her troupe in 1990 – the same year she received the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award, one of India's highest performing arts honours.
Vithabai successfully campaigned for government pensions for Tamasha artists. But many of the hardships she knew persist today, says Marathi writer Pradnya Daya Pawar.

Troupes spend nearly eight months a year on the road, with performers struggling to feed their children and educate them, she says. Despite government aid, many remain indebted to private moneylenders.
Vithabai's financial struggles persisted until her death in January 2002. Her family could pay only 4,000 of the 5,900 rupees owed to the Pune hospital where she died, the Times of India reported.
Fellow artists and admirers chipped in to bring her body home to Narayangaon.
Maharashtra has since instituted a lifetime achievement award in her name.
Eetha could now introduce Vithabai to a generation that never saw her perform, though the changes to her name have left some uneasy.
Marathi writer Pragya Daya Pawar argues that omitting the reference to Vithabai's caste risks obscuring the difficulties she confronted.
"It erases the social location, struggle and resistance that shaped her remarkable journey, reducing an extraordinary artist's story to a purely individual achievement," she says.
But Bansode, who spent years performing alongside her mother, says there is much to celebrate.
"The name doesn't matter to me. I am simply proud that a film is being made about my mother," she says.

articles.title: Nigeria's 'ultimate hard man' who become an online meme
articles.summary: Before becoming a household name in the Nigerian film industry, Edochie built a career in broadcasting.
body: For generations of Nigerians, Pete Edochie was more than a celebrated actor.
He was Okonkwo – the fierce, proud and troubled warrior whose portrayal in Things Fall Apart made him a household name and earned him a place in the hearts of millions.
Even in death, many Nigerians still refer to him by the character's name, a testament to the enduring impact of a role that defined his career.
Edochie died on 25 November, aged 79, in the south-eastern Nigerian city of Enugu following a prolonged battle with prostate cancer.

In 1987, Edochie starred in a television adaptation of Chinua Achebe's acclaimed novel. His portrayal of Okonkwo would change his life, establishing him as one of Nigeria's most respected actors and bringing him international recognition.
The series depicted the struggles of an African community as British colonial rule and Christianity began to transform its traditional way of life.
Joy Nnamdi, a fan of both the novel and its television adaptation, believes Edochie was the perfect choice for the lead role.
She said nobody else could have brought the character to life as convincingly.
"His character Okonkwo gave a face to the highly celebrated novel," she told the BBC in Nigeria's biggest city, Lagos.
The role also cemented his reputation as a hard man, a screen persona he would maintain through much of his career.
"It was very rare to see him laugh in movies. He was the ultimate tough man," Nnamdi added.
With his deep, authoritative voice, imposing presence and effortless command of African proverbs, Edochie had a way of dominating a scene without raising his voice.
Whether playing a village elder, a wealthy businessman or a feared traditional ruler, he became an enduring embodiment of patriarchal authority on screen.
Edochie went on to become one of the most recognisable faces of Nollywood, Nigeria's film industry, which has grown into one of the world's largest.
From Kenya to South Africa, MultiChoice's Africa Magic channels helped take his films into millions of African homes as Nollywood became a cultural phenomenon across the continent.
Although many of his films were rooted in his Igbo culture, their themes of family loyalty, inheritance disputes, spiritual beliefs and the abuse of power resonated with audiences far beyond Nigeria.
Before becoming a household name in the film industry, however, Edochie had built a successful career in broadcasting.
Born on 7 March 1947 in Zaria, northern Nigeria, he attended primary and secondary school in Kaduna before studying journalism and television at the School of Journalism and Television in the UK.
He joined the Eastern Nigerian Broadcasting Corporation in 1967, the year Nigeria's civil war broke out.
He joined the pro-separatist Voice of Biafra, and recently described the war years as the greatest personal challenge he ever faced.
"During the war, the experience that we had as Biafrans, you know, survival was difficult. Hunger was driving us into eating all sorts of nonsense," he recalled.

He rose through the ranks to hold senior management positions but then switched to acting. Over a career spanning several decades, he appeared in numerous films, including Igodo, Rituals and Billionaire's Club.
Pete Edochie starred in Netflix's first original Nigerian film, Lionheart
His career also bridged the transition from home-video productions to global streaming platforms.
The 2018 romantic comedy Lionheart, which became Netflix's first original Nigerian film, introduced his work to a wider international audience.
He also worked in Ghana, where he starred alongside some of the country's biggest film stars in the 2017 comedy John and John.
His contribution to the arts was recognised in 2003 when he received one of Nigeria's national honours, the Member of the Order of the Niger (MON).
He also received several other accolades, including the Industry Merit Award at the Africa Magic Viewers' Choice Awards.
In recent years, Edochie found an unexpected new audience online.
His distinctive facial expressions, witty remarks and memorable scenes from his films became popular social media memes, introducing his work to a younger generation of Africans.
For many who had never watched Things Fall Apart or his early Nollywood films, his stern expressions became a humorous way of conveying disbelief, disapproval or exasperation at everyday situations.
But his reputation as a formidable screen presence was no joke to those who grew up watching him.
Sani Muazu recalls that parents in the northern Nigerian city of Kano would sometimes invoke Edochie's name to keep misbehaving children in check.
"They would tell you: 'Okonkwo will come and visit you if you don't stop' and we would begin acting right," he said.

"To be honest, we grew up scared of him. Even though he was on the screen and not physically present, some of his roles added to our fears because he played some popular occultic roles, and villain roles suited him."
Edochie's expressions were sometimes used as online memes
Tributes poured in from fans and fellow actors following news of his death, with many describing him as a giant who helped shape Nigeria's film industry.
Popular actress Genevieve Nnaji paid her tribute in a post on X.

"I will let the assurance of the fact that you are a chosen one; and therefore, have returned to the most high God override my grief and heartbreak. May the heart of a true lion forever rest in peace. We love you," she wrote.
Patience Ozokwor, popularly known as Mama G, who appeared alongside Edochie in several productions, remembered him as a brilliant actor and a source of wisdom.
"He has been a father to stories that are told, like an elder sitting down telling you how things were done in those days," she told BBC News Pidgin.
"I called him any time, any day. He'll tell you what to do and what not to do."
Film director Babangida Bangis told the BBC that Edochie's death was a loss not just for Nigeria or Africa, but for the global film industry.
"Just days ago, during a seminar for filmmakers across the country, his name popped up as an example of brilliance on the screen, longevity and professionalism," he said.
"I think his loss is one for the world, not just Nigeria or Africa. We all grew up watching and loving him."
Nigeria's President Bola Ahmed Tinubu also mourned the veteran actor, describing his death as a major loss to the country's film industry and cultural heritage.
The president, like many admirers, singled out Edochie's portrayal of Okonkwo, saying the performance and his subsequent roles had established him as one of Nigeria's most accomplished actors.
But beyond the fame and formidable character he portrayed on screen, his family remembers a man whose greatest legacy was the importance he placed on honesty and speaking the truth.
Leo Edochie, his son, told the BBC that his father was a strong-willed man.
"Of all his legacies, I think the whole world would agree that these two were the most important: telling the truth and remaining honest," he said.
He described his father as a man who lived an exemplary life, offering a model that young people could learn from and aspire to follow.
"I don't really have a choice, but the truth is that I have to carry on that legacy for our family," he added.
Edochie's influence also extended to his family, with two of his six children, Yul and Linc Edochie, following him into the Nigerian film industry.
Yet, for an actor so closely associated with stern expressions and intimidating characters, some of his most endearing moments came when he let his guard down.
In 2021, he made a brief appearance in music star Phyno's video for the song Highway, surprising fans with a display of dance moves that showed a lighter, more playful side of the septuagenarian.
It was a refreshing reminder that the man behind the formidable screen persona could also laugh, dance and enjoy himself.

articles.title: Costa Rica bars UN rapporteur on Palestinian territories from entering the country
articles.summary: Francesca Albanese, leading critic of Israeli abuses in Gaza and West Bank, barred on ‘national security grounds’
body: Costa Rica has barred entry to the UN special rapporteur on the Israel-occupied Palestinian territories, Francesca Albanese, earning the ire of the UN human rights chief.

Albanese, an Italian national, went to Costa Rica to receive an honorary doctorate from the University of Costa Rica. She was stopped at the airport in San José on Thursday and not allowed to enter the country, and was only transferred to a hotel on Saturday, shortly before her departure for Mexico.

The UN human rights office said that Albanese had been stopped from entering the country on “national security grounds”. Costa Rica’s migration office said its decision had been made after she was the subject of an “alert” over alleged ties to terrorism.

The UN high commissioner for human rights, Volker Türk, said he was “deeply concerned” by the decision to deny Albanese entry. “This is difficult to reconcile with Costa Rica’s longstanding commitment to human rights,” he said.

Albanese shared a picture on X of her suitcase by an airport bench, where she was meant to stay the night. “Second night in the airport. Guarded by security at every step. Uncomfortable chairs. Noise. Bright light,” she posted.

Albanese, who acts as an independent expert appointed by the UN human rights council, has been outspoken on Israeli abuses in Gaza and the West Bank. She has drawn ire from Israel and its allies for being one of the first, most prominent officials to accuse Israel of committing genocide in Gaza – which Israel denies.
Related: ‘Systematic assault’: paramedics blocked and attacked by Israeli settlers and soldiers in West Bank

The US placed sanctions on Albanese and revoked her visa for her work on Palestine in the summer of 2025, cutting her off from the global financial system. The sanctions make daily life a struggle for Albanese, who has no access to western banks or credit cards.

Albanese called for an investigation into whether her denial of entry into Costa Rica was connected to the US sanctions, speaking remotely at the ceremony for the acceptance of her honorary doctorate.

Costa Rica’s government, headed by the rightwing president Laura Fernández, is close to the Trump administration and has cooperated with it on security and immigration issues. The government has also intensified its ties with Israel.
Israel’s envoy to the UN, Danny Danon, praised Costa Rica for its decision, accusing Albanese of using her UN position to spread propaganda against Israel.

Albanese arrived at Mexico City’s international airport at about 10.30am local time (4.30pm ⁠GMT) on Saturday, where supporters with Palestinian flags offered her a bouquet of flowers and met her with a regional musical band.
She delivered Friday’s university keynote lecture remotely while being held for two nights at San José airport.
“Goodbye, for now,” Albanese posted on social media early on Saturday with a photo of herself on a plane holding her passport. “I’ll be back, I promise, when Costa Rica is again free.”

articles.title: ‘Victory for democracy’: Taiwan’s ruling party secures best result in a decade
articles.summary: DPP nearly doubles number of constituencies it controls, with outcome expected to anger Beijing
body: Taiwan’s ruling party secured its best result in a decade in Saturday’s local elections, doubling the number of constituencies it controls, in an outcome expected to anger Beijing.
The Democratic Progressive party (DPP) won 10 of Taiwan’s 22 mayoral and county magistrate races, up from five in its disastrous showing in the last local elections four years ago.

The DPP is led by Lai Ching-te, Taiwan’s president, who is detested by Beijing. The Chinese Communist party (CCP) regards Lai as a “separatist” who opposes its plans to unify China and Taiwan. China regards Taiwan, a self-governing island, as part of its territory, a stance that the majority of Taiwanese people reject.
Taiwan’s main opposition party, the Kuomintang (KMT), won 10 races, down from 14 in the last vote. But it retained control of Taiwan’s capital, Taipei, and the neighbouring New Taipei.

The local elections were fought mainly on bread-and-butter issues such as housing costs and wealth distribution rather than cross-Strait relations. Nevertheless, “China will be breathing a sigh of relief” at the KMT’s success in Taipei and New Taipei, said William Yang, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group.
The KMT promotes closer ties between Taiwan and China and the annual Taipei-Shanghai forum is one of the only major remaining exchanges between China and Taiwan.

The race for Taipei mayor had been a close contest between the KMT’s incumbent, Chiang Wan-an, and Puma Shen, a DPP legislator who has faced sanctions from China. On Saturday afternoon, thousands of supporters gathered outside Shen’s campaign office to watch the results come in.

The mood started optimistic, with chants of “Puma, keep going!” and “Turn it around!”, but as Chiang extended his lead, a sombre mood descended. Shortly before 8pm, Shen took to the stage to concede defeat, greeted by a prolonged standing ovation.
“The results are in and I’ve lost,” Shen said. Visibly emotional, Shen emphasised that he would continue to work hard.

“Tonight, the people of Taipei made the best decision. As I made clear in previous interviews with foreign media, no matter who wins today, it is a victory for Taipei and a victory for democracy,” he said.
Shen, a criminologist turned politician, is also the co-founder of Kuma Academy, which runs civil defence courses for Taiwanese people to prepare for a potential Chinese invasion.

Yan Jing-na, 50, a Shen supporter, cried after he conceded defeat. “I don’t care which party he belongs to. As long as he puts Taiwan’s interests first, I’ll support him,” she said, adding that she thought it was “cool” that Shen was labelled a “Taiwan independence separatist” by Beijing.
“He has long defended Taiwan’s rights,” she said, “and that’s why I have to support him, because the people of Taiwan have had it tough.”
Related: ‘We’re not freaks’: police raid sparks concern for Taiwan’s LGBT-friendly image

Yan said Shen had helped raise public awareness of China’s campaign against Taiwan.“So we’re not worried. I think many people are now more aware of China’s influence on Taiwan because of him,” she said.

Taiwanese officials raised the alarm over thousands of incidents of suspected misinformation or election interference before Saturday’s vote. There have also been reports of hundreds of China-linked AI-generated videos spreading disinformation about Taiwanese politicians disliked by Beijing.

China has also maintained physical pressure around the island. Taiwan’s defence ministry said that 33 Chinese warplanes and eight warships had encircled Taiwan on Friday. China’s Taiwan Affairs Office has not yet commented on Saturday’s results.
Lai, Taiwan’s president, said in a Facebook post that he thanked “the people of Taiwan for their support and trust in the DPP’s nominated candidates”. Lai did not mention China in his statement.

Zhan Ying-yi, 51, another Shen supporter, said that he was “disappointed” in the result, “but that’s how democracy works”. “We can only respect the outcome. After all, we still have the freedom to vote and that is something we should cherish,” he said, adding that the election result had heightened his concerns about the threat posed by China.
“There’s only one thing I fear: that one day we might be ruled by the People’s Republic of China. Then we would lose everything.”

articles.title: Google told to cease building Belgian datacentre over lack of planning permit
articles.summary: Greenpeace report shows US tech firm has continued construction despite a planning appeal being unresolved
body: Belgian authorities have ordered Google to halt construction work on a large datacentre in the south of the country because the US tech firm’s requests to modify the original terms of the planning permission did not have approval.

“Inspectors visited the site and observed that the building was almost finished, with the structural work completed, even though the permit had been refused,” Raphaël Stokis, a Wallonia regional official, told the public broadcaster RTBF.

Stokis said the 300 workers had been given a verbal order to stop work that had been confirmed in writing to Google. The company said in a statement it was “committed to maintaining an open and collaborative dialogue” with the regional authorities.

Google’s 2025 application to change its plans, notably including a switch from air- to water-cooling, was initially approved by local authorities but later revoked after protests. The company has appealed and a ruling is due early next year.

The vast building, which occupies about 3 hectares (7.4 acres) of a 50-hectare business park on the site of a former coalmine at Aiseau-Presles, about 9 miles west of Charleroi, is one of three originally planned by Google on the site.

Nicolas Yernaux, a regional government spokesperson, told Agence France-Presse on Friday that a report was being submitted to public prosecutors alleging “a major offence: the illegal construction of a building covering 3 hectares”.
The environmental group Greenpeace earlier this week published a report including drone footage that showed Google was carrying on construction work at the site despite lacking the correct permits.

“The tech giant is continuing work, even though in August the latest version of its planning permission to build this datacentre was revoked,” Greenpeace said, adding that it had filed an emergency appeal with local planning authorities.
“The climate crisis will only intensify in our region,” the environmental group said. “Against this backdrop, the construction of energy-guzzling behemoths cannot be allowed to go unnoticed.”
Related: How datacentres are driving an illegal mining rush in the Amazon ‘more devastating than gold’

Google’s 2024 permit was to construct three smaller air-cooled datacentres, but in 2025 it applied instead to merge two of them into one much larger facility and switch to liquid cooling by drawing 600m3 of water an hour from the nearby Sambre River.

The regional administration initially approved the amendments in April, but residents and protest groups appealed and in August the Wallonia infrastructure minister, François Desquesnes, revoked the modified permit over drought concerns.

Google appealed against that decision to Belgium’s council of state and a ruling in the case is expected on 7 January. A company spokesperson said on Friday: “We have halted works consistent with the direction from local authorities and pending additional guidance.

“We have operated in Belgium for over 15 years and remain committed to complying with local laws and an open, collaborative dialogue with government officials and all relevant authorities about our work in Wallonia.”
The legal row is the latest confronting the company in Europe as large tech companies push to build datacentres to support the AI boom.

In October, Finland opened a criminal investigation into possible breaches ⁠of environmental ⁠laws ​at a planned Google datacentre in the rural north of the country. Work has been halted until environmental impact assessments are completed.

articles.title: Trump crackdown shatters US hopes for Guatemalans displaced by climate crisis
articles.summary: As drought worsens, more climate migrants are trekking north – but as US deportations ramp up, rural Guatemalans are running out of options
body: The small plots of farmland in Caparrosa, an Indigenous Maya Ch’orti’ village in eastern Guatemala, are bone dry. It’s mid-June, and the rainy season should have started a month and a half ago, but it’s barely rained at all. The maize is just a few inches tall, and some plots are completely bare.

Lidia Molina is nursing her two-and-a-half-year-old daughter, Karla, sitting on a dusty step next to skinny dogs and chickens. “We haven’t planted our maize yet; it’s too dry,” Molina, 30, said. “We’re hoping it will rain soon, or else we’ll have to make do with whatever my husband sends us.” She is thin and her daughter weighs only 19lb (8.5kg), more typical for a nine-month-old.

The Maya Ch’orti’ have survived centuries of forced displacement and ethnic cleansing by colonial settlers and feudal landowners, maintaining their traditional subsistence way of life despite losing land, water sources, ancestral knowledge and language.

But climate breakdown has pushed them to the brink. Guatemala is one of the top 20 countries most vulnerable to climate change, with two-thirds of the population expected to face water shortages by 2050, according to the United Nations Environmental Program (Unep). Indigenous peoples, who account for nearly half Guatemala’s population of 19 million, are often found in the most remote regions without basic infrastructure such as tap water or irrigation systems. It is these areas that are facing the most severe climate impacts.

In the past 15 years, as erratic rainfall causes subsistence crops to fail, thousands of Guatemalans, many of them Indigenous, are believed to have taken out loans or pawned small plots of ancestral land to fund migration to the United States in hope of finding work to save their families from starvation.

Donald Trump, in his second stint in the White House, has ramped up deportations of migrants, many of whom who had been living and paying taxes in the US for years, severing an economic lifeline for their families back home. Now, as rainfall grows even more unpredictable and dries up regional agricultural labor opportunities, rural communities in Guatemala are running out of options.

Caparrosa, where Molina lives, is located in the ancestral homeland of the Maya Ch’orti’ people, and is one of thousands of tiny rural communities in what is known as the Dry Corridor, a 1,000-mile stretch that covers almost a third of Central America, from southern Mexico to Panama. It’s a spectacular, mountainous and relatively dry area.

For millennia, the dry corridor’s six-month rainy season began in early May, with a relatively dry spell midway through, known as the canicula. Millions of Indigenous and non-Indigenous subsistence farmers timed their plantings – maize, beans and other basic foods – to this seasonal rainfall. Few communities had water capture or irrigation systems.

By the 2000s, the changing climate began to have devastating effects, when heavy rain and flooding caused catastrophic damage in the area. These crisis conditions helped persuade the government to pass its 2013 climate change framework law, making Guatemala the second country in the Americas – after Mexico – to pass explicit climate legislation.
Then came the drought. The rainy season came later and later, and the canicula got longer, hotter and drier.
By 2019, five years of failed harvests had left 1.2 million people in the region needing emergency food aid. Children were dying from malnutrition.

Lidia Molina and her husband, Brian Pérez, are not their real names, which the Guardian is not disclosing, for their security. They were surviving at that time on just a few tortillas each a day, and several of their children showed signs of malnourishment, including distended bellies and hair loss.

The relentless drought triggered the first wave of mass climate displacement from the dry corridor: 188,000 Hondurans and 185,000 Guatemalans traveling in family groups were detained at the US southern border in 2019, an eightfold increase from 2016.
By 2021, the drought had intensified and the situation in Caparrosa was desperate, and so was Pérez.

To escape the worsening drought, Pérez was about to embark on one of the most dangerous migrations in the world with his 10-year-old son Wilson, traveling more than 2,000 miles (3,300km) through Mexico to get to the US border.

To pay his “coyote”, a local guide for informal migration routes, Pérez had handed over the deed to the land where more than a dozen people, the entire extended family, live in a cluster of modest adobe shacks. The land would serve as collateral for a loan to cover the passage, which Pérez hoped to pay off once he found a job in the US.
Fast forward to June 2026. Pérez was not in Caparrosa. Wilson was, and he was 16 by now. The skinny teenager was taller and more solemn and he had a migration nightmare to recount.
The journey across Mexico was really tough, he said, but the US was worse.

Then US president Joe Biden had ostensibly stopped the family separations at the border that surged during Trump’s first term, but that was not the reality Wilson and many others encountered. “They didn’t let us cross, and separated me and my dad,” he told the Guardian.
Biden had also continued enforcing title 42, Trump’s pandemic-era executive order to automatically turn away most asylum seekers without hearing their cases.

Exhausted after a month traveling overland, Pérez and his son Wilson were taken away separately and detained by the US border authorities in a large multi-storey detention center in Texas. Their American dream was over before it had even begun.
