“It was really hard [in detention], not much food or water,” Wilson said. “I didn’t see or speak to [my dad] for two months, until they sent us back to Guatemala.”

Since then, his father has been spending long periods away from home, working south of the US border to keep the family from destitution – and to pay back the debt he owes the coyote. He has travelled as far as southern Mexico to work on banana plantations, and sometimes his family don’t know where he is or when he’ll be coming back.

Pérez’s absences mean more responsibility on Wilson to help his grandfather and uncles in the fields when he’s not in school. He held out a large plastic bowl full of maize kernels, saved from last season’s meager crop, ready to plant when it rains again. “It did rain a little a couple of weeks back, but we’d been too busy day laboring for other farmers, so our land wasn’t ready for planting,” said Wilson. “Anyway, we don’t have enough money for fertilizer yet.”

Ironically, synthetic fertilizer is mostly made from the same fossil fuels that, when burned, are the main driver of the greenhouse gas emissions causing global heating – and turbo-charging the drought and erratic rainfall in the Dry Corridor. The cost of synthetic fertilizers has also surged thanks to the illegal wars in Ukraine and Iran.

A week or two later, an update came through from Lidia Molina that Wilson had finally planted the maize after a lightning storm soaked the earth, more than 50 days late. But the rain didn’t last, and not long afterwards they lost the whole crop, Molina said, because the maize was too small and fragile then to endure the canicula.
Yet some communities in the region have found ways to adapt to the changing climate.

In another Ch’orti’ village, Corozal Arriba, just 15 miles north across the mountains from Caparrosa, farming families are producing an abundance of organically farmed fruits and vegetables: tomatoes, eggplant, peppers and potatoes.

Amid the worsening drought, and with no international aid or climate finance or government funding for long-term adaptation measures, the community worked with a grassroots Ch’orti’ organization called Comundich in recent years to build three relatively simple and cheap reservoirs and an irrigation system to pipe in water from a mountain spring. It was a process of trial and error, learning from YouTube videos and local agronomists, but the reservoirs have been a gamechanger: malnutrition and forced migration rates are way down, residents said.
Comundich has helped build almost 20 reservoirs across the territory so far, but there are hundreds of Ch’orti’ villages like Caparrosa where farmers are still 100% dependent on the rain.
Then in late June, just after Wilson planted the maize, which then failed, Pérez got in touch. He was in the United States.

Ten days earlier, he had crossed over the border near the Mexican city of Juárez and its west Texas sister city El Paso, on the other side of the international line that follows the Rio Grande. He had traveled overland for four weeks with 20 or so other Ch’orti’ subsistence farmers, all struggling to support their families. Pérez said that this time he’d used his father’s land as collateral to pay the same coyote, whom he now owes 145,000 quetzales, or almost $20,000.

“I really tried in Guatemala,” Perez said. “And I went to Mexico, working long, hard days in extreme heat in the banana plantations so the coyote wouldn’t take out the house. But you can’t get ahead, and I want more for my family. The weather has changed, it doesn’t rain when it should, and out there it’s just you, the crops and God.”

Droughts, floods, extreme heat, desertification and other climate-related disasters forcibly displaced 250 million people globally over the past decade, the equivalent of 70,000 displacements every day, according to the UN refugee agency. There is no reliable data on how many people from the Dry Corridor have been displaced – internally or across international borders – by climate change. But in the past decade and a half, thousands of poor rural Guatemalans on the frontlines of climate breakdown are believed to have traveled north in hopes of reaching the US.
Under current international law, neither climate change nor famine alone are considered legitimate justifications for claiming asylum.

The US is the biggest historic emitter of the greenhouse gases that cause climate breakdown. It also has a track record of protecting fossil-fuel interests while delaying or blocking action on funding for climate adaptation or reparations being paid by wealthy polluting countries to compensate for climate-driven loss and damage in poor countries like Guatemala.

“Now that I made it to America, little by little I’m going to pay off the debt, and after that the coyote will return the deeds to my mom and dad,” Pérez said. “I’ll only stay until I’ve saved up to make improvements to my house, and then I’ll go back to my family.”

Pérez is aware that the Trump administration is carrying out raids across the US to detain and deport immigrants. He is taking precautions, and rarely goes out except to work as a kitchen hand in a Chinese restaurant, hoping for the best.

Meanwhile, Jorge Cruz, who is from Guayabo, a Ch’orti’ community south-west of Caparrosa, also used his family’s farmland as collateral to head for the US in 2021 and ended up working in construction in Minneapolis. (Cruz is a pseudonym to protect his identity.)
By 2025, he was sending money home to his wife every two weeks and slowly paying off the debt he owed the coyote.

But early one morning last September, he and a colleague were surrounded by ICE trucks after stopping at a gas station to buy coffee and breakfast sandwiches before work. Cruz was arrested, and spent 70 days in an ICE detention center in Wisconsin, before being deported back to Guatemala wearing the same clothes he’d had on that day in September. He lost all his belongings, including the keyboard and guitar he played in the church band, he said.

About a third of Guatemalans put on deportation flights in 2025 had been employed in construction, according to the Guatemalan Institute of Migration, with others working as pilots, accountants, house painters, farmers, mechanics, electricians and waiters, and a whole host of other professions that contributed to the US economy. They were paying US taxes and sending billions of dollars to the Guatemalan economy through remittances.

Trump’s mass deportation campaign shows no sign of abating, despite the drubbing by Democrats in the midterm elections and his anti-immigration tactics being a factor in turning voters against the Republicans.
Still, Pérez, in the United States, is hopeful. In mid-November, he said he had just finished paying off his debts and could now start saving to build a decent house in Caparrosa.
“It’s not easy, but if I keep my head down I think I’ll be fine. It’s a risk, but Wilson is grown now. If something happens to me, he will look after his siblings.”

Cruz, however, speaking to the Guardian in Guatemala City, where he found work in construction after being deported back to Guayabo, said: “I felt like crying when they sent me back with nothing, without having achieved my goal to provide for my children and build a better house.” He added: “But I still have that American dream.”
In the past, deportees would try to reach the US again, but the current immigration crackdown is so cruel that Cruz said, for now, returning feels too risky.

His family home, like most in Guayabo, consists of a couple of simple dusty adobe rooms, with an outdoor toilet, kitchen and sink with tap water a couple of days a week. There are a few bigger, more western-style houses that belong to neighbors with relatives who made it in the US.

For Cruz, like Pérez and most other Guatemalan climate migrants, the expensive and dangerous trek to the US wasn’t a first, second or even third choice. Speaking outside his workplace in Guatemala City, Cruz said he hadn’t finished paying back the loan for his journey, and the coyote still had two land deeds, one for a half-acre plot that Cruz bought after years of working in the sugar plantations. The other is an acre plot owned by his father, Don Clementino, that had once belonged to his grandfather.

“It worries me that the coyote could come here at any time,” Don Clementino said at his home in Guayabo. “That one acre is where I plant corn and beans for the family. The climate isn’t the same any more, so it doesn’t yield much of a harvest, but that’s the only land I have to leave to my children.”

Guayabo is rockier than Caparrosa and particularly arid, with few natural springs and limited access to clean water for drinking, cooking and hygiene. Parasites and other gastrointestinal diseases are common, as are worms and insects that burrow into the skin.

Forced migration is the norm. Historically, a lot of men and boys from Guayabo would spend six months a year working in the sugar cane fields on the Pacific coast. Others have crossed the border to Honduras for the coffee harvest. Both crops involve backbreaking work for low wages, which is relied upon by many Indigenous Guatemalans, who have the highest rates of poverty and child malnutrition in Latin America, according to Unicef.

Mario Ramírez, 58, also of Guayabo, has traveled to Honduras each year to harvest coffee since he was just 11. Back then, the going rate was half a quetzal (50 cents) for every box of coffee beans harvested, a rate that has risen gradually to 20 quetzales ($3).
“The pay is better now, but there’s no coffee to pick because of the weather. The rains have changed,” Ramírez said.

Like subsistence farming, these commodity crops are on the decline due to climate change. And with migration to the United States growing more difficult, the people of Guayabo are left with few options.

Guatemala is suffering far more extreme weather events, drought, floods, and higher temperatures, while the latest El Niño cycle is expected to be punishing. Yet the average rainfall nationally hasn’t really changed over the past few decades. According to Edwin Castellanos, Guatemala’s vice-minister of natural resources and climate change, this presents opportunities.

“The problem is water distribution, and the solution is storage, which isn’t expensive,” Castellanos said. “The ministry of agriculture has programs to promote water storage and irrigation, but the challenge is reaching thousands of farmers. Guatemala is a small country, and we don’t have sufficient resources or personnel.”

Rodimiro Castillo, founder of the grassroots Maya Ch’orti’ group Comundich, believes that the Dry Corridor can be productive and provide a dignified life for the Ch’orti’ people. But only if the approach to adaptation is more radical and begins to address some of the historical injustices dating back to land seizures and ethnic cleansing by colonial settlers and the military dictatorship, which has left large swathes of ancestral Ch’orti’ territory in the hands of private landowners.

“There is water, but it is not in the hands of those who need it, it is in the hands of those who seized it,” said Castillo. “So we are trying to break this narrative that life is not possible in our territory, the Dry Corridor. It is possible.”

The improvised irrigation system in Corozal was proof of concept for Comundich, which is now pitching project ideas to the government and international aid agencies, pushing for more focus on long-term sustainable adaptation measures rather than short-term handouts.

articles.title: Two Médecins Sans Frontières staff killed by Israeli strike in Gaza, charity says
articles.summary: MSF and head of WHO denounce attack on Gaza City clinic as Israel claims security guards were members of Hamas
body: Israeli forces have bombed a clinic run by Médecins Sans Frontières in Gaza City, killing two of its staff members, the organisation has said.

MSF said Israel had directly struck the clinic, despite the fact that its location was known to the Israeli military and that it was well marked with MSF logos. The organisation denounced the attack and said that with the deaths of the two security guards on Saturday, Israel had killed 17 of its staff members during the war in Gaza.
The head of the World Health Organization, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, condemned the bombing, saying: “Those risking their lives to save others must be protected, not attacked.”
In a post on X, Ghebreyesus also said: “Attacks on health facilities, health workers and humanitarian personnel in Gaza are outrageous and unacceptable … These attacks MUST STOP.”

The Israeli military claimed that the two men whom they killed, Ahmad Abou Hassira and Moaz Alitsbach, were members of Hamas’s military wing. It also added that the strike was “not directed at a hospital” and had caused no damage to the facility.

The Israeli military has often accused Hamas of embedding itself within civilian infrastructure, including hospitals. However, in 2024 the head of the international criminal court’s Palestine investigation said claims about the presence of Hamas fighters in Gaza’s hospitals had been “grossly exaggerated”.

Israel has killed Palestinian medical workers en masse since the start of the war in Gaza. According to the Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics, at least 1,700 have been killed by Israeli attacks. Rights groups say the Israeli military has engaged in systematic destruction of civilian infrastructure, including medical infrastructure.
The UN has repeatedly called on Israel to stop its restrictions on the entry of supplies to allow Palestinians to prepare for the winter and begin to rebuild the destroyed strip.
The result is a healthcare system “experiencing systemic collapse, severely undermining its capacity to meet the basic health needs of the civilian population”, according to a UN report in August.
The humanitarian situation is also deteriorating, as heavy rains exacerbate crowded and unsanitary living conditions, leading to the spread of infectious diseases.

Israel has continued to bomb Gaza on a near-daily basis despite a ceasefire signed in October 2025, killing at least 1,705 people since then. Israel has repeatedly accused Hamas of violating the understandings of the ceasefire.
The war began after a Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023 that killed about 1,200 people.

More than 74,000 people have been killed and more than 175,000 injured in Israel’s war in Gaza. A UN independent international commission of inquiry found that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza and that Israeli officials, including the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, incited these acts. Netanyahu is separately wanted by the international criminal court for war crimes. Israel denies these claims.

articles.title: Spain to vote in election that could put far right in power for first time since Franco
articles.summary: Socialist PM Pedro Sánchez’s high-stakes gamble could end in defeat to a coalition including the far-right Vox
body: Spaniards head to the polls on Sunday to vote in a high-stakes snap general election that could put a far-right party in government for the first time since the country’s return to democracy after the death of Gen Francisco Franco in 1975.

Although the next election was not due until summer next year, Spain’s socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, called the vote in October after three rightwing and far-right parties voted down the emergency legislation that his government had proposed to address the country’s housing crisis.

Huge public anger over soaring rents exploded in September after the eviction of María del Carmen Abascal, an 87-year-old woman who was removed from her home in Madrid because she could not afford the 230% rent increase demanded by the investment fund that had bought her apartment.

Faced with nationwide protests, Sánchez’s coalition minority government put together a package of measures aimed at improving access to housing, from a ban on evictions until 2030 to the regulation of temporary lettings and lettings by room.

Sánchez opted for one of his characteristic gambles and announced the early election after the proposals were torpedoed by the conservative People’s party (PP), the far-right Vox and the rightwing Catalan separatist Junts.
Related: Why all of Europe should be watching as Spain’s far-right Vox closes in on power | Eoghan Gilmartin

The prime minister – an inveterate risk-taker whose penchant for unpredictable moves has fuelled his political survival – calculated that his opponents’ decision to block the housing overhauls could work in his electoral favour.
On Friday morning, Sánchez said he was confident of victory. “I can’t conceive of us losing,” he told Cadena Ser radio, adding: “When progressive Spain gets going, it’s unstoppable.”

But while his Spanish Socialist Workers’ party (PSOE) has managed to narrow the distance between it and the PP, which is leading the polls, to fewer than three percentage points, the right looks likely to form the next government in coalition with the far right.

Survey after survey predicts the PP will finish first but fall short of a majority, leaving it dependent on a deal with Vox. Between them, the two parties are forecast to secure a joint majority well above the 176 required seats in Spain’s 350-seat congress of deputies. Even if the PSOE enjoys a last-minute surge and comes first, the parliamentary arithmetic suggests it would struggle to cobble together another coalition administration with the support of its allies in the leftwing Broad Front alliance and with that of regional nationalist parties.

Choosing housing as a key battleground allowed Sánchez to attempt to shift the focus away from the corruption allegations facing his inner circle. It also offered him the chance to move on from his government’s much-criticised handling of the crisis in Spain’s north African territory of Ceuta, which was sparked when about 80,000 people crossed into the territory from neighbouring Morocco in the space of 48 hours.
But some of the energy of the government’s resurgent campaign was sapped at the end of October when 69 people were killed in Spain’s second deadly rail crash in just nine months.

The PP and Vox have used the two crashes to accuse the government of failing in its basic duty to keep Spaniards safe. More broadly, the PP and Vox are using the poll as a referendum on what they disdainfully refer to as “sanchismo”. They argue that the style of government favoured by the prime minister and his allies is cynical, corrupt, opportunistic and self-serving.
“Spain deserves a decent prime minister and [Sánchez] isn’t one,” the PP leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, told viewers during a head-to-head debate between the two men last week.

Sánchez, however, insisted that while he had made errors, Spain was in a better state than it was when he came to office in 2018. “My government hasn’t been perfect; I’ve made mistakes,” he said. “But I’m also fully aware that we have always governed in the right direction.”
The prime minister has also sought to depict the snap election as a stark choice between progressive forces and reactionary ones – as typified by the PP’s putative alliance with Vox.

“You must decide whether you want our country to move backwards or continue moving forwards, and whether you prefer a government that works for the interests of the majority of society,” he told Spaniards as he announced the vote.
Related: Race hate exploded in this Spanish town last year. Now its residents are bracing for more

Over recent days, the government has tried to underline its commitment to social justice and equality by proposing a new tax on fortunes of more than €100m (£84m) that would help fund childcare, housing and public services.

The PP, meanwhile, is promising to lower taxes, build 1m homes, and “restore the country’s ambition and self-esteem”. Vox’s manifesto, which includes plans to have Sánchez and his government prosecuted “for treason and crimes against the security of the state” over the Ceuta mass crossing, focuses on deregulation, “remigration” and giving Spanish-born people priority over those born abroad for housing and public services.

Although the PP’s previous leader, Pablo Casado, famously repudiated Vox and its ideology, accusing the party of practising a politics based on “fear, anger, resentment and revenge”, the PP has repeatedly entered into regional coalition governments with Vox and now runs four of Spain’s autonomous regions with the party.

In recent days, the PP and Vox have attempted to call into question the fairness and transparency of the election, making baseless claims that the government may seek to rig postal votes. Vox’s leader, Santiago Abascal, has also suggested, without providing evidence, that Sánchez is working to undermine democracy and change the country’s demographic makeup.

articles.title: Palestinian tells of ‘devastating’ struggle after being made redundant by EU in Gaza
articles.summary: Mohammad Baraka unable to access redundancy payment for almost 20 years’ service as family’s situation becomes ‘increasingly desperate’
body: A Palestinian man who worked for the EU in Gaza has told of a “devastating” struggle to survive after he was made redundant by bosses in Brussels.

He was let go last year after being evacuated to Egypt but his redundancy payment was made to an account to which he has no access. “My family’s situation has become increasingly desperate,” said Mohammad Baraka, a former staffer at the EU border assistance mission (EUBam).
“Both of my daughters have suffered severe psychological distress as a result of the war, displacement and the prolonged uncertainty surrounding our future.”

The 220,000 Israeli shekels (£52,000) payment for almost 20 years’ service was made on 5 August last year to the Bank of Palestine but access to the money has been blocked, a risk he was aware of given the relatively large sum being transferred.

He said he wrote on several occasions to the European Commission, asking it not to make the payment into that bank because of a known risk that a large sum of money could be misconstrued as war funds. “I am now in the devastating position of having money in my name that I cannot access, while my family is experiencing severe financial hardship,” said Baraka.
Instead he had asked for the payment to go to a new account in an Abu Dhabi bank, but that never materialised.

Baraka was evacuated in 2023 after his house in Gaza was bombed and family members killed. The EU tried to relocate him to alternative offices in the West Bank but travel for Palestinians in Gaza was severely restricted. After a hasty three-day concession agreed with the Egyptian government, Baraka was able to leave for Cairo.

As the conflict continued, Baraka was initially able to work remotely from Cairo as an EU employee and had the comfort of a salary, private healthcare and access to schools for his two children. But when Brussels decided to close its EUBam office in Rafah, he was let go, leading to what he says have been traumatic consequences for himself and his wife and two daughters.

He says the evacuation to Egypt with no plan for onward travel to an EU nation or a diplomatically secured place in another country has rendered him stateless, with no residency rights and no right to healthcare or schooling for his seriously ill wife and two daughters, both of whom he says are suffering from the trauma of war.

One of his daughters has an acute mental health condition and Baraka says he cannot pay for her treatment. “I am not asking for charity or special treatment. I am asking for access to my own money, and for accountability over a decision that could have been avoided,” said Baraka.
“I had specifically asked the [EU] mission to transfer my money to my new bank account in Egypt to avoid precisely this situation,” he said.

“If the EU argues that it fulfilled its obligations simply because it transferred the settlement, I believe the legitimate question is whether an employer can consider its responsibility discharged when it knowingly disregards an employee’s repeated warnings about the destination of such a substantial payment.”

Last year he wrote to the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, pleading with her to reverse what he called his “unjust dismissal” and asked her to restore his employment, even temporarily, “until a dignified and legal solution is arranged”.

He also wrote to the European ombudsman to ask them to open an investigation but they replied last week to say they had no scope for an inquiry. “We fully appreciate that you and your family are in an immensely difficult position. The hardship you are experiencing as a result of the war and your displacement are clear from your complaint,” wrote Tina Nilsson, the head of inquiries.

“I realise that this conclusion will be disappointing. I nevertheless hope you can understand why, based on the information available, there are insufficient grounds for the ombudsman to intervene further.”
He is now suing the commission for alleged breach of Belgian employment law but the case could take years to be heard.
Without the “laissez-passer” document that allowed him to be evacuated from Gaza, he cannot leave Egypt, he says, putting him in an impossible position.
A spokesperson for the commission said: “Due to the ongoing related court case, we cannot comment on this further.”

articles.title: Yuri and I used to play football together. Then I spotted his name among Russia’s war dead
articles.summary: I had no idea he had gone to fight in Ukraine and without hacked data I would probably never have learned of his death
body: One evening, after weeks spent counting Russia’s war dead, I began looking for names I might recognise.

My colleagues and I had been working our way through more than 11m death certificates leaked from Rosstat, Russia’s state statistics agency, and identifying nearly half a million Russian soldiers who had died in the war in Ukraine.
We had sorted the dead by age, region and cause of death, building the most detailed picture yet of Russia’s losses in nearly five years of war.
Now I typed in the names of the places where I had grown up.

My childhood was spent in Rublevka, a stretch of pine forest west of Moscow that has been home to the Russian elite since Soviet times. With the collapse of communism and Russia’s chaotic embrace of capitalism, the dachas of party officials gave way to the sprawling estates of oligarchs.

Vladimir Putin and Dmitry Medvedev established their residences in Rublevka. In more recent years, the area has become a refuge for ousted leaders, among them Ukraine’s Viktor Yanukovych and, as the Guardian previously reported, Syria’s Bashar al-Assad.
I did not expect to find many names there.
Related: Russia’s war dead: the hidden toll of the Ukraine conflict

Our analysis had shown just how unevenly the burden of the war had fallen across Russian society. In some of the poorest regions, working-age men were up to 32 times more likely to die in the war than men of the same age in Moscow. I knew sons of the Russian elite who had left the country shortly after the invasion, keen to avoid being called up to fight.
My village, Zhukovka, returned no results.
I worked my way along the Rublyovo-Uspenskoye highway, the well-paved road connecting the wealthy settlements west of Moscow. Here and there, a lone death certificate appeared.
Then I typed in Gorki-10, a town a few miles further down the road, named after the famed writer Maxim Gorky, who spent his final years there.
One of the names on my screen was instantly familiar: Yuri Vladimirovich Kyrmyz, aged 31.
Place of death: Makiivka, Svatove district, in the Russian-occupied Luhansk region of Ukraine. Cause of death on 3 February 2025: an explosion during military operations.

Makiivka, a small village on the banks of the Zherebets River, had been the scene of months of bitter fighting as Russian forces sought to retake territory lost during Ukraine’s 2022 counteroffensive.
Two decades earlier, Yuri and I used to play football together as teenagers.

Though we were never particularly close, he was a reliable presence at our games, a quiet, unassuming defender who rarely had much to say. We had not spoken in years. Until that evening, I had no idea he had gone to fight in Ukraine, let alone that he had died there.
I also do not know what made him join Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The Kremlin has worked hard to insulate Moscow and its suburbs from the war. In neighbouring Barvikha, at the Luxury Village shopping complex, visitors can still buy a Ferrari or a Chanel handbag, despite western sanctions. But for all its associations with wealth and power, Rublevka is also home to another Russia.

Parts of Gorki-10 consist of Soviet-era blocks of flats, built for families who serviced the rich or toiled at the local stud farm, which dates back to the 19th century. I remembered that Yuri’s family was not well-off. Before enlisting, Yuri worked as a car dealer.
The signing bonuses and salaries offered by the Russian military, in some cases amounting to several times the average annual wage, would have represented a life-changing sum of money.
He may also have believed in the war.

Yuri was one of millions of Russians of our generation who grew up immersed in the memory of the Soviet victory over Nazi Germany. Victory Day, on 9 May, was one of the biggest occasions of the year, rivalled only by New Year’s Eve. Over the past two decades, Putin has appropriated that collective memory, telling a new generation of Russians that in Ukraine they are fighting the same “Nazi” enemy their grandfathers once faced.

Until I discovered Yuri’s name in the database, the only person I knew to have joined the invasion, other than the soldiers I had interviewed in the course of my reporting, was my former football coach Andrei Solomatin.
In his prime, Solomatin had played for CSKA and Lokomotiv Moscow, won 13 caps for Russia and appeared in all three of the country’s matches at the 2002 World Cup.

But his life unravelled after retirement. There were debts, problems with alcohol and a gradual slide into obscurity. By the time I met him, the former international footballer was eking out a modest living coaching our local Sunday league team.

Our team was an eclectic collection of nationalities, including Dutch (me), British and Nigerian players. I cannot recall Solomatin ever expressing hostility towards Ukraine. Politics, as far as I could tell, did not concern him.

In autumn 2022, he began delivering aid to Española, a far-right military formation drawn from the ranks of Russian football ultras fighting in occupied Ukraine. By July 2023, he had joined the unit himself.

He was back on television, this time in military fatigues. In interviews, he spoke of his “complete trust” in Putin. The war appears to have given him a sense of public importance he had not enjoyed for years.

Yuri, like hundreds of thousands of other Russian soldiers who have died in Ukraine, left little public trace. Had hackers not obtained the records of Russia’s state statistics agency, I would probably never have learned of his death.
Although in some of the worst-affected parts of Russia nearly everyone knows someone who has died in the war, the full scale of the losses remains hidden from the Russian public.
Asked about the military deaths on Wednesday, the Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, dismissed the findings, insisting that only official data could be trusted.
Independent Russian journalists were quick to point out the irony, given that the figures came from the Russian state’s own statistics agency.

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: Zelenskyy criticises Trump for calling Putin his ‘friend’; Kyiv deploys new laser weapon
articles.summary: Ukrainian leader likens Putin to Hitler; laser system intercepts Russian drone but not ready for ‘mass deployment’. What we know on day 1,739
body: Volodymyr Zelenskyy has criticised Donald Trump for calling Vladimir Putin his “friend”, likening the Russian leader to Adolf Hitler. “Of course it’s up to the president of the United States, but ... it’s strange,” the Ukrainian leader told the BBC in an interview aired on Friday. “He is an aggressor, and a killer... He can’t be a friend. Just cannot be. It’s the same that somebody says about Hitler during the second world war, that he’s a good friend. No. He’s not a friend.” Zelenskyy said what was needed was “more progress” and urged Washington to increase pressure on Moscow.

Ukraine has for the first time used a laser weapon to shoot down a Russian jet-powered drone, according to its state-backed defence group Brave1. An adviser to Zelenskyy, Serhiy Beskrestnov, published footage earlier this week showing a target crashing in a fireball, saying a Russian Geran jet drone had been shot down by a laser system known as Blysk for the “first time”. Agence France-Presse quoted Brave1 as saying on Friday: “Footage recently emerged online showing a Ukrainian laser system being used in combat to intercept an enemy jet-powered drone.” But Brave1 cautioned that “a first successful interception does not mean the technology is ready for mass deployment”. “Laser air defence remains an experimental technology,” it said, adding that at least seven teams in Ukraine were working on laser weapons.

Ukraine on Saturday reported hundreds of Russian drones fired at several regions, with one person killed and five injured. Zaporizhzhia military administration chief Ivan Fedorov said more than 700 Russian drones had been fired at the region over the past 24 hours. Russian authorities said more than 1,200 Ukrainian drones had been shot down overnight, with hundreds aimed at the Moscow region, while the governor of Bryansk region ‌said a Ukrainian drone struck a bus ​in the village of Klimovo, wounding nine people.

A convoy of Russian ships carrying military vehicles bound for Libya has turned around in the Mediterranean after Ukrainian maritime drones sank ⁠a Russian naval warship in Benghazi ⁠port last Sunday, Reuters quoted ​three people from military and security services as saying on Friday. The convoy, which was escorted by the Russian navy frigate Golovko, turned around near the strait of Sicily on the same day as ⁠the attack in Benghazi, said a European military official who had been tracking the convoy. A Ukrainian military intelligence official and a Middle East security official confirmed the flotilla had turned from heading to Libya. Russia’s defence ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Ukraine has offered ⁠a Black Sea ceasefire to enable food ⁠exports and ⁠passed this ​on to international allies, the foreign minister ⁠said. “We are ready for ⁠a ceasefire. We are ​grateful to ‌India, Turkey and ‌Egypt, which are playing ‌an active and important role in de-escalating tensions in the Black Sea, as well as in mediation efforts. ‌We are now awaiting a response from ​Russia,” Andrii Sybiha was cited by public broadcaster Suspilne as saying on Friday. He added that Russia had proposed ⁠Ukraine suspend attacks on the ​Russian ​oil sector under ​the truce, but ​Kyiv ‌would only consider ​this ​as part of a bigger energy ceasefire deal.

Ukraine’s military said on ⁠Friday it ⁠had struck ​a Russian solid ⁠rocket fuel production site ⁠in ​the Tula ‌region south ‌of Moscow ‌overnight. “The plant is the starting point of the ‌missile production chain: it manufactures ​components for plastic explosives and ⁠the polymer used ​to produce ​solid ​propellant for ​Russian ‌ballistic missiles,” ​the ​defence ministry said on Telegram.

Russia’s foreign ministry has accused ⁠Latvia of creating artificial ⁠obstacles ⁠to hinder the ​transit of Russian grain to ⁠global markets, saying the restrictions pose additional risks ⁠to global food security. Ministry ​spokesperson ‌Maria Zakharova ‌claimed in a statement published ‌on the ministry’s website on Friday that Latvia was conducting inspections of Russian grain shipments for allegedly ‌stolen Ukrainian agricultural products and was seeking ways ​to ban Russian grain transit altogether.

articles.title: Men dominate this Japanese game. One woman broke a 100-year-old barrier to rise to the top
articles.summary: Tomoka Nishiyama will soon compete against men in professional shogi, often known as Japanese chess, but women remain marginalised in the popular game
body: Encouragement was in short supply when, in the 1960s, Akiko Takojima set her sights on becoming an elite shogi player. Women were too “stupid” to excel at the Japanese board game, a male instructor told her, before suggesting she find something else to occupy her time.

Decades after Takojima and five others became the first female professionals, a 100-year-old barrier in the game is about to be broken. From April, Tomoka Nishiyama will turn shogi’s gender bias on its head when she becomes the first woman to compete against men at the highest level of the game.

“Senior women players have always been kind to me,” Nishiyama, 31, told reporters after announcing she would become a kishi, a gender-neutral classification that, nonetheless, has featured only male players since the Japan Shogi Association was formed in 1924. “They have also taught me about the difficulties of being a woman in shogi.”
Related: Golden ginkgos and rich red maples: Japan’s autumn colours – in pictures

A Yomiuri Shimbun editorial hailed her promotion as “a new era” in the world of shogi, but with the exception of Nishiyama, women are still marginalised in professional shogi and among the ranks of amateurs.

“Even today, there are far fewer girls playing than boys,” says Saori Shimai, a professional shogi player in the women’s game, who began learning shogi at the age of six after watching her grandfather play.
“When I was learning shogi there were hardly any girls playing at all,” says Shimai, who is also executive director of the Ladies professional shogi players’ association of Japan.

Often referred to as Japanese chess, shogi is thought to have originated in India before spreading to China and other parts of Asia. Playing on a rectangular board comprising 81 grids, each player manoeuvres their 20 pentagonal pieces as they aim to checkmate their opponent’s king and win the game.
About 5 million Japanese play regularly, according to a 2025 government white paper, but only about 20% are women.

When the shogi association relaxed the promotion criteria last year to allow women to become kishi based solely on their results in all-female tournaments, several male professionals raised objections, while Nishiyama was subjected to abuse on social media. Some attempted to dismiss her advancement as “affirmative action”, prompting the shogi association to intervene in her defence.

The notion that male players are naturally superior persists, right down to commentary arrangements, in which the resident expert is invariably male. Last year, the Japan shogi association prohibited pregnant players from playing in title matches for 14 weeks around their expected due dates but was quickly forced to scrap the rule.

“There need to be other big changes to how shogi is organised so that they reflect how women live their lives,” says Karolina Fortin, the first foreign player to turn professional, who fell in love with the game as a puzzle-obsessed child. “Long overdue things, like maternity leave and childcare.”

Fortin says she was delighted, but “anxious”, about Nishiyama’s achievement. “There’s no doubt that she’s made history … But the road ahead will be difficult. She will be surrounded by male players so will need to keep proving herself.”

The introduction of women’s professional shogi in 1974 was a reminder of how far the game has come. “The boys I had played against as an apprentice had agreed that if they lost to me they would have to pay a fine or shave their heads,” Takojima said in a 2019 interview with Shukan Bunshun magazine, referring to a traditional display of contrition in Japanese culture.

The upper echelons of the elite game have long struggled to reflect growing interest among women. As of October, there were 174 active players with the kishi rank, all of them men. That will change when Nishiyama takes up her new status next year. The number of female professionals, who compete against each other, has risen from the original six to more than 80, but they are still outnumbered by men.
Shimai, who turned professional when she was 15, says she had always believed it was “only a matter of time” before a woman started competing in the same professional category as men.

“The number of female professionals has increased, and the standard of play has dramatically improved,” she says. “Attitudes are gradually changing. Women were often assumed to be weaker players, but the perception gap is narrowing. But we want to do more to create an environment in which women can enjoy shogi.”

Itsuko Hayashi, a shogi instructor, believes those involved in the game are beginning to accept players on merit, irrespective of their gender. “I think the shogi world respects strength,” says Hayashi, a member of the women’s association, which arranges events to promote the game among women and girls. “Male players have no problem recognising shogi ability among women.”

As she prepares to make shogi history next spring by competing against men in title matches, Nishiyama says she has been inspired by a desire to take on stronger opponents, and by the women who had come before her.
“I recognise that I’m someone who can help create a new milestone in the history [of shogi]. I’m very aware that the history built up by those players is what allowed me to get to where I am today.”

articles.title: Canada’s top court upholds Quebec law barring public sector workers from wearing religious symbols
articles.summary: Closely watched decision exposes tensions between minority rights and the power of government to override those rights
body: Canada’s top court has largely upheld a controversial secularism law in the province of Quebec barring public sector workers from wearing conspicuous religious symbols, in a closely watched decision that exposes the tensions between minority rights and the power of government to override those rights.
In a 6-1 ruling released on Friday morning, the supreme court found Quebec was permitted to shield the law, Bill 21, from most court challenges on the grounds that it violated charter rights.
“Bill 21 is rooted in Quebec’s legitimate and historical commitment to ensuring the laicity of the state in a free and democratic society,” chief justice Richard Wagner wrote in the majority opinion.

Canada’s top court says the four days of hearings from earlier in the year marked one of the longest in its 151-year history. Fifty-one interveners participated, including six attorneys general – also a record number. The court’s website crashed on Friday morning when the judgment was released.
While the judgment was celebrated by some in Quebec who considered it a vindication of the province’s fight, it was swiftly criticised by religious civil liberties groups.

“We cannot exist in a country as free people, where governments can literally go to the electorate and say, ‘I’m gonna take away the rights of a certain group of minorities’, because it’s popular and to play wedge politics with the charter rights of Canadians,” Stephen Brown, chief executive of the National Council of Canadian Muslims, told reporters at a press conference. “If that is the case, we don’t have a charter of rights and freedoms. We have a charter of suggestions and permissions.”

Passed in 2019, Quebec’s secularism law, Bill 21, bars workers including lawyers, judges, police and teachers from wearing religious symbols such as a hijab, turban, kippah or a cross while on the job.
Related: ‘It shut all my doors’: how a Quebec law banning religious symbols derails women’s careers

Central to the case – and the reason provincial governments across the country are closely watching the result – is the “notwithstanding clause”, a constitutional mechanism that allows elected governments to override certain fundamental rights and freedoms guaranteed by Canada’s Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

The clause is the result of political compromise from the 1980s, when the federal government set out to replace the existing British North America Act with a new constitution. Provinces feared that under a new constitution, courts would become too powerful, undermining the authority of the elected government. A compromise was hashed out: in cases when a government – provincial or federal – felt that the courts had overstepped, they could invoke the clause to override certain charter rights of citizens.

Some fundamental rights, including protections of religious freedom, equality and speech, could be suspended. But voting, as well as language rights, were untouchable, ensuring Canadians could remove a government if they wanted. A government could only invoke the clause for five years. Before they could renew it, they would first have to face voters.

In its decision, the supreme court rejected most arguments that Bill 21 violated portions of the charter that are not subject to the notwithstanding clause, including guarantees relating to the equality of men and women and the education rights of Quebec’s English-speaking minority.

Quebec’s use of the clause with Bill 21 was notable – and controversial – in that it was the first time the notwithstanding clause had been invoked pre-emptively in an attempt to shield the law from court challenges. Quebec also passed Bill 96, which sought to strengthen French language protections – again pre-emptively invoking the notwithstanding clause.

But groups affected by those laws can still challenge them and many teachers, religious and civil liberties groups argued it was a clear violation of constitutional rights and reflected government overreach. Quebec’s government has defended the law, saying it is constitutionally valid.

In April 2021, a Quebec superior court judge described the effects of the law as “cruel”, saying it “dehumanises” the people it targets, but conceded the statute could not be struck down because it was protected by the notwithstanding clause. Quebec’s court of appeal also upheld the law in February 2024 on the same grounds.

In its 520-page judgment, the court did find that element of the law infringed on democratic rights protected by the charter, including preventing elected members of Quebec’s National Assembly who wear face coverings for religious reasons from participating in the legislative process.

In a 4-3 decision, the court also endorsed the ability of lower courts to issue “judicial declarations” on laws protected by the notwithstanding clause, giving judges the power to declare a law in violation of the charter, even though the law would be permitted to stand.
The court’s decision was celebrated in Quebec, where the governing Parti Québécois has looked for wedges with the federal government and institutions like the supreme court.
The premier, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, had previously said his province’s right to decide its own laws was at risk.

Canada only recently fended off a threat to national unity after voters in Alberta rejected the initial stages of a separatist push. But Quebec’s newly elected government has shown an eagerness to clash with the prime minister, Mark Carney.

The supreme court’s judgment comes on the same day an appeal will be heard regarding a superior court decision that forces Quebec’s members of the national assembly to swear allegiance to King Charles to sit in the Salon Bleu – the chamber of the assembly. Lawmakers from a number of parties in the province recently refused to swear the oath of allegiance.

articles.title: Ahmad Shams obituary
articles.summary: Other lives: Iranian doctor and writer twice imprisoned in his home country before settling in the UK
body: My father, Ahmad Shams, a doctor, writer and political activist, who has died aged 97, was twice imprisoned in his home country of Iran before eventually resettling in the UK. Having spent his life campaigning for democracy and equality, Ahmad treasured what Britain gave him. He admired the NHS as a socialist venture made real, and he took part in British democracy with real pride, voting in every general election.

It was in London that he completed his six-volume history, Struggle for Freedom and Independence in Iran, spanning the eve of the Arab conquest to 2009. Published anonymously and freely online in Farsi, it reflected his belief that knowledge belonged to everyone.

Born in Tabriz, Iran, Ahmad was the son of Zahra-Soltan and Ghassem, the official dentist to the Qajar crown prince’s court. Ahmad’s elder brother Ismail was one of the leaders of the Soviet-backed Azerbaijan People’s Government (1945-46), a briefly autonomous state inside northwestern Iran. Inspired by his brother, Ahmad, who went to Ferdowsi school in Tabriz, joined Iran’s communist Tudeh party in his early 20s, but challenged its subservience to Moscow and was expelled. Nevertheless, he remained a socialist, on his own terms.

He studied medicine at Tabriz University, and in 1953 married Najibeh Farajpour-Azar. After the coup that overthrew the elected prime minister of Iran that year and restored the shah to power, Ahmad was imprisoned for his political activities for six months. He continued his medical studies behind bars, and shortly after his release opened a surgery, treating poorer patients for free.

In 1970 Ahmad qualified as a paediatrician at Tehran University, and continued to write and publish anonymously on ideas of democracy and equality. While in Paris taking a course in paediatric respiratory medicine, he published The Past Is a Lamp Lighting the Path to the Future (1977), a chronicle of Iranian history between the coups of 1921 and 1953.

When the 1979 revolution that overthrew the shah led to the establishment of another dictatorship, the Islamic Republic, Ahmad organised resistance. Arrested and sentenced to death in 1981, he survived because the prisons needed doctors, and was released after six years. He resumed practising medicine until his late 60s.

In 2000 he left Iran with Najibeh to join their sons in Uxbridge, west London. In 2012 they moved to Richmond. During this time Ahmad worked on his last and largest piece of work, the study of Iran’s struggle for freedom, which he published online in 2023.
Najibeh died in 2021. Ahmad is survived by their two daughters, Solmaz and Golnaz, and two sons, Siamak and me, and by nine grandchildren.

articles.title: ‘Mass-casualty event’ in Europe possible amid rise in Russian sabotage, says thinktank
articles.summary: Report warns attacks on critical infrastructure could lead to demand for retaliation and expose EU divisions
body: Russian sabotage attacks on Europe are increasing and a “mass-casualty event” is now possible as increasingly skilled operatives target critical infrastructure with ever more complex methods, a leading strategic thinktank has said.

The International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) said in a report that Russian intelligence services and their proxies were targeting European railways, energy networks and defence industries in an attempt to weaken support for Ukraine.

Russian sabotage had risen by 16% in 12 months and the use of arson and explosive devices had doubled, the IISS said, “presenting a risk of mass-casualty incident … as the space for miscalculation narrows”, and of subsequent retaliation and escalation.

While unskilled ⁠recruits were still carrying out most operations, a semi-skilled tier of operatives were now using more intricate methods, ​including improvised explosive devices with ‌timed and remote detonators, the report said.

National authorities across Europe had arrested proxies, expelled intelligence officers and sometimes closed Russian consulates, but there was “no clear evidence that these measures have made sabotage a less attractive instrument of Kremlin policy”.

“Arrests remove ‌proxies, but are highly unlikely to deter the Russian intelligence services that direct ‌them,” it said, with attacks by “layers of intermediaries” coming “in surges, concentrated on strategically important countries and sectors”.

The IISS said Germany and Poland would remain the most targeted states, as their transport and industrial networks were crucial to supplying Ukraine. Targeting of critical infrastructure accounted for more than half of incidents over the past 12 months.

The report said 29 Moscow-linked incidents were recorded in Poland between October 2025 and September 2026, including a November 2025 incident in which an explosive charge damaged a railway line used for delivering supplies to Ukraine.

In Leipzig, Germany, on 4 August, a drone laden with explosives was discovered near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo aircraft used for military supplies. Investigators ‌suspect a second drone collided with a DHL cargo plane soon after air traffic was suspended.
Related: Russian national charged with spying on Silicon Valley tech and defense firm

The IISS said the key question facing Europe was whether it could turn a series of national decisions in response to specific incidents into a Europe-wide strategy before “an operation conducted by the RIS [Russian intelligence services] or proxies causes a mass-casualty event”.

An operation that caused fatalities or serious disruption would “generate demands for retaliation” and could expose divisions between EU governments, it said, with none having set red lines despite recent attacks in Estonia, Lithuania and Romania.

The possibility of a mass-casualty attack – whether deliberate or by miscalculation – raises “concern about escalation [being] the primary instinct”, the IISS said, calling for Europe to “publicly signal what level of harm triggers which response”.

Moscow has rejected out of hand all accusations from western governments and intelligence services that it is behind a Europe-wide campaign of drone, cyber, arson and explosive attacks aimed at undermining and disrupting EU support for Ukraine.

articles.title: Momentous decision looms after judges call for Netanyahu charges to be dropped
articles.summary: Dropping of corruption charges against Israeli PM after unusual intervention could set damaging precedent
body: The Israeli judges presiding over Benjamin Netanyahu’s corruption trial have called on prosecutors to end proceedings, a highly unusual intervention that leaves the attorney general facing a momentous political decision.

The prime minister has been charged with bribery, fraud and breach of trust in three complex and overlapping criminal cases that hinge on his relationship with telecoms magnates and other wealthy businessmen. Ending the trial without a ruling could set damaging precedents for media independence and how politicians are held to account.

“There were evidentiary difficulties in the case, but the position the judges laid out effectively means abandoning the media to the whims of politicians and publishers, and setting an impossible bar for conviction in corruption cases,” said Yael Freidson, the legal correspondent for Haaretz, who has covered the trial since it began in 2020.
Related: ‘Systematic assault’: paramedics blocked and attacked by Israeli settlers and soldiers in West Bank

The judges urged prosecutors to drop one case because “the chances of a conviction are low”, seek a plea deal in a second, and reconsider the third set of charges. Even if prosecutors were to prove the allegations of fraud and breach of trust in that case, it was not clear that Netanyahu’s alleged behaviour amounted to criminal conduct, they said.

The attorney general, Gali Baharav-Miara, who was summoned to court to hear the judges’ statement in person, must now decide whether to accept their recommendations and end a trial that has dominated and shaped Israeli politics for the best part of a decade.

The decision is not straightforward, even though the current bench has in effect indicated a not guilty verdict is a foregone conclusion. If the trial continues, their ruling could still be appealed to a higher court, where fresh judges could take a different stance.

“[The former prime minister] Ehud Olmert was acquitted on all charges by the district court and was subsequently convicted by the supreme court on a minor charge,” Ben Caspit wrote in Maariv. “It ain’t over till it’s over.”

“[Baharav-Miara] could opt to reach a lenient plea bargain agreement with the defendant and put it all to rest, but that would be an admission of the entire justice system’s failure and would further fuel the conspiracy theories that Netanyahu and his disciples have been pumping ever since he was indicted.”
Settling or dropping all charges would immediately and permanently absolve Netanyahu, ending the threat of jail time and dispelling the legal shadow hanging over his political future.
A bill making its way through the opposition-controlled parliament would in effect bar him from serving as prime minister until the trial was concluded.

Netanyahu, who has pleaded not guilty to all charges, claims he is the victim of a political witch-hunt and welcomed the judges’ recommendation as a vindication. “The truth has finally come to light,” he said.

Baharav-Miara has withstood pressure from the judges in the case twice before. In 2023 and in 2025 they urged prosecutors to drop bribery charges, the most serious ones that Netanyahu faces, although they stopped short of suggesting the whole trial should be wrapped up.

Perhaps the single point of agreement between Netanyahu’s supporters and his critics in relation to the trial is concern that it has been allowed to drag on for too long. Testimony from Netanyahu had extended over a year and a half, across 98 hearings, the longest by a single witness in Israeli judicial history, Freidson said. The transcripts from all the hearings run to more than 60,000 pages.

Oren Persico has sat in every hearing since the case began in 2020, covering it for the investigative magazine The Seventh Eye. Over that period he watched the judges slowly lose control of their courtroom, he said.

“It started with giving the defence a lot of rope to do what they wanted. Netanyahu’s lawyer lashed out at the prosecution and humiliated them, almost every day, and attacked the judges, which should be an absolute red line in court,” he said. “I think the judges are afraid and tired; they just want to get it all over with.”

The sense of a bench cracking under pressure was exacerbated by the recommendation to reconsider charges in one of the cases against Netanyahu. These were laid out by prosecutors seven years ago, and have not changed since, prompting joking questions about whether the judges had even read the indictment, and serious ones about their political judgment.

When Netanyahu was indicted, he decided to fight the charges both inside and outside the courtroom, declaring war on the prosecution, the media, the police and key democratic and judicial institutions, Persico said.

“To keep himself out of jail, he tried to form an authoritarian state here in Israel, which tore apart society. I understand the interest in putting an end to that,” Persico said. “But ending the trial would send a terrible message to criminals and politicians and media bosses: that if you fight strongly enough you can get away with anything.”

articles.title: At critical juncture, Friedrich Merz finds Germans’ support for Ukraine wavering
articles.summary: German chancellor is on difficult terrain, at home and abroad, as he fights to maintain European backing for Kyiv
body: The German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, is navigating choppy waters both at home and abroad over his insistence that Europe must keep up support – both military and financial – for Ukraine.

At a Brussels summit on Thursday, Merz reiterated his view that all EU member states – pointedly, “not 23 or 24” – should support a €45bn (£38bn) loan for Ukraine for 2027. He has threatened to veto the bloc’s budget unless all countries sign up to the loan, a stance that saw him accused of “classic blackmail” by Robert Fico, the populist prime minister of Slovakia. Czechia, Hungary and Bulgaria have also voiced their misgivings, to varying degrees, over Berlin’s dogged position.

But, unhappily for Merz, he cannot rely on the wholehearted support of the German public, either. A new survey released this week showed that, for the first time, Kyiv no longer enjoys majority support among the German population. The study by the Körber Foundation, showed 53% of those questioned were against Germany supporting Ukraine militarily, with only 46% in favour – compared with 59% just a year ago.

Merz, whose disapproval ratings stand at a record 88%, is therefore looking increasingly isolated. This all sends a worrying signal to Kyiv, which has counted on Germany as its biggest backer for some time, since Washington largely withdrew its favour.

The government’s attempts to push the case for Ukraine domestically now, when it is arguably most necessary, are not helped by the fact that German leaders have been reluctant to play up the support Germany has given to Kyiv since 2022 for fear of stoking embers of resentment.

This extends to keeping as quiet as possible about the estimated 1.33 million Ukrainians who have been given refuge in Germany since the full-scale invasion of their country, because of the strong tendency of the far-right, anti-immigrant Alternative für Deutschland to portray them as a burden.

As the cost of living crisis bites and the German public feels increasingly poorer economically, the debate over Ukraine funding is being framed – misleadingly, say critics – as a contest between the nation’s living standards and the billions paid to Ukraine’s defence.

This week Merz faced down opposition MPs in the Bundestag, the most vociferous from the pro-Kremlin AfD, who called for funding to Ukraine to be halted, as parliament debated the budget for 2027, Germany’s largest ever, due to be voted on by the weekend.

Opposition, however, is not only coming from the right. In Saxony-Anhalt, where in December the AfD may take over a state premiership for the first time, the BSW, a small, Russia-friendly, leftwing party, last month teamed up with the AfD to also demand a halt to arms supplies to Ukraine and the lifting of economic sanctions against Russia.
And on Thursday, an influential former Protestant church leader, pacifist and theologian, Margot Käßmann, called for a “change of course” and more diplomacy from the government.

“We must do everything we can to prevent war,” Käßmann said in an interview with DLF, a public broadcaster, insisting she would not bend to demands for Germans to defend themselves, instead calling for “much more diplomatic commitment”. She also accused Merz of not taking the “discomfort of the population seriously”.

Notably, the Körber survey found that the lowest support for Ukraine, 31%, was recorded in Germany’s eastern states, where the AfD – nationally five points ahead of Merz’s conservative CDU/CSU alliance in the polls – has an increasing hold on power. Only 11% of east Germans are in favour of military help to Ukraine, while 75% would like to see a “normalisation” of relations with Russia, the survey found.
Merz now faces an uphill battle to win the German people round to his own government’s conviction that support for Ukraine is vital if Germany is to ensure its own security and future.

articles.title: Friday briefing: Will the proposed ban on conversion practices make it over the line?
articles.summary: In today’s newsletter: ​The draft bill currently being scrutinised by MPs faces a growing backlash, but nearly a decade after its proposal LGBTQ+ people are still waiting for protection
body: Good morning. There is broad consensus from LGBTQ+ advocates, mental health professionals and politicians that trying to change a person’s sexual orientation or gender identity against their will is abhorrent. For decades, campaigners have fought for a UK-wide ban on conversion practices, which can result in lasting trauma and alienation for victims.

Now, after years of delays, a ban finally looks within reach, with a draft bill currently being scrutinised by a committee of MPs and peers. But opposition has intensified in recent months from those who believe this could inadvertently criminalise parents, teachers and counsellors who ask questions about a young person’s gender identity. Meanwhile, campaigners argue there’s a world of difference between a sensitive discussion and abuse.
I spoke to our social affairs correspondent Jessica Murray about the developing row, but first the headlines.

UK politics | Labour’s internal divisions over the giant Rosebank oilfield have spilled into the open, with nearly 100 Labour MPs writing to the prime minister to express their opposition to the project.
Ukraine | EU leaders were bracing for a clash over long-term financial aid for Ukraine amid an effort to finalise high-stakes budget talks by the end of the year.

US news | Donald Trump has alleged without evidence that economic figures published by the US federal government before this month’s midterm elections were “fake” and demanded an investigation after voters roundly rejected his Republican party.
UK news | A bill to implement the UK-EU deal will grant significant powers for ministers to enact even closer ties with Brussels, though it will stop short of Labour’s red lines.

Europe news | Gérard Depardieu has been ordered to stand trial on a charge of raping a female actor at his Paris home in 2018, after an appeals ⁠court rejected his attempt to avoid having the case tried.

Jeanette Winterson’s powerful semi-autobiographical novel Oranges Are Not the Only Fruit draws on her experience of conversion practices, including violent exorcism, at the hands of her strict Pentecostal community in the north of England in the 1970s.

It’s tempting to view what was then described as “conversion therapy” through a historic lens, or associate it only with strict religious views. But conversion practices are far from a thing of the past: research by Stonewall last year found that 17% of LGBTQ+ Britons have experienced physical assault, 10% have experienced “exorcism” practices and 12% experienced “corrective rape” or sexual assault, all in an attempt to change their sexuality or gender identity.
When I asked Winterson about the proposed ban a few years ago, she told me: “Any country with equal rights should be banning conversion therapy. To me, it’s as bad as forced marriage.”
Eight years have passed since a ban on conversion practices was first pledged as part of Theresa May’s LGBT action plan, but fell apart amid moves to exclude trans people.

A similar commitment was included in Labour’s 2024 manifesto, but campaigners have become increasingly frustrated by the government’s reluctance to engage with the issue since the supreme court ruling on biological sex – which does not impact legally on a proposed ban.
The Scottish government also scrapped its plans to ban conversion practices via stand-alone Holyrood legislation, but will work with UK ministers on a UK-wide ban.

But in an interview with Jessica this week, the equalities minister Bridget Phillipson insisted Labour remains “committed” to the principle of the bill – in the face of growing criticism that the proposed bill could criminalise parents and healthcare professionals, or stifle free speech.

The draft bill, published in June, proposes the new offence should satisfy three elements: the intent to change an individual’s sexual orientation or gender identity, conduct that amounts to abuse, and that causes the victim serious harm. The third element in particular sets a pretty high bar for prosecution.

People found guilty of conversion practices would face up to five years in prison, an unlimited fine, or both. Courts would also be able to issue protection orders if someone is at risk of an abusive practice, including conduct outside England and Wales.

This happened to Shash Appan, who, at 16, was sent to stay with her grandparents in India after conflict with her family over her sexuality and gender identity. She was told the visit would last two weeks, but remained there for two years – during which time she was isolated, unable to travel alone and denied access to a phone or the internet.

“They wanted me to conform to what they saw as normal or natural,” Shash told Jessica. “They removed any form of gender expression. They would cut my hair, go through my belongings. I was only able to leave after convincing them to let me go and be homeless – they thought I’d come crawling back but I’ve stayed away since.”

Supporters argue that, while some elements of conversion practices, like physical assault, are already illegal, drawing them together under a blanket ban would give victims stronger legal protections as well as acting as a deterrent.

However, the bill has prompted criticism from some faith leaders. The Church of England, which has supported a ban on conversion practices relating to sexual orientation since 2017, says legislation must not “unintentionally criminalise providing appropriate prayer and pastoral care to those who seek it”, while the Catholic Bishops’ Conference of England and Wales has called for the bill to be abandoned.

The gender-critical campaign group Sex Matters has also called for the bill to be withdrawn, arguing campaigners haven’t demonstrated a need for it and that it would cause “an immense amount of collateral damage.” Hilary Cass, the cross-bench peer and paediatrician who wrote a landmark review into young people’s gender services, also withdrew her support, claiming it was already having a “chilling effect” on healthcare professionals and their ability to conduct “appropriate and ethical therapy.”

Some campaigners supporting a ban are also worried that the framing of “abusive” practices suggests that some attempts at conversion are acceptable. Others want stronger safeguarding provisions, so that the burden does not fall on victims to come forward.
Will it criminalise parents or healthcare workers?

Much of the opposition to the bill relates to the inclusion of gender identity in the ban, and many of the voices ranged against it are those who oppose trans-inclusive single sex spaces – a position reinforced by last year’s supreme court ruling.

The Telegraph has also launched a campaign to scrap the draft bill, running articles claiming that supportive parents could be arrested under a ban, GPs would be at risk of sanction and that the scale of conversion practices is “vastly overestimated”.
And, separately, the Guardian has heard from parents worried that the proposals could make sensitive family interactions with counsellors or social workers much harder to navigate.

But Phillipson was adamant the ban will not affect ordinary parenting “Normal parenting will not be affected,” she told Jessica. “Parents will continue to be able to have frank conversations with their children.”

Jessica describes some of the scenarios she’s come across where parents have crossed the line into abusive behaviour: “I’ve heard from people who had their hair forcibly cut off, or were threatened with corrective rape. That’s what the bill is trying to stop.”

Phillipson also stressed that therapists and counsellors will still be able to ask rigorous and exploratory questions. And the Ban Conversion Practices Coalition is keen that the final bill should include detailed notes to explain what is and isn’t covered, so the law can’t be undermined by vexatious complaints.

Prime minister Andy Burnham also reiterated his commitment to the ban earlier this week, albeit underlining the need for “very careful” pre-legislative scrutiny. Between the lines, Jessica says “they’re clearly leaving the door open for amendments and changes.”

The draft bill is only at the committee scrutiny stage and, as critical voices get louder and a growing number of Labour MPs put on record their opposition, “the backlash could get a lot bigger”, she predicts. Campaigners are broadly optimistic, but there’s still fear that, if it becomes more contentious, this government that is determinedly focused on easy wins and “breathing space” issues may back off. Does the long grass beckon?

This matters not only to those campaigning for an inclusive ban but to the wider community. For trans folk, it means yet another stressful public debate about whether they should be included in protections afforded to everyone else. But in recent years I’ve reported on the steady roll-back of rights across LGBTQ+ lives, in terms of safety, funding, and access to services. My sense is that this bill has come to mean more than the sum of its parts – a rare ray of hope for an embattled community.
